maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the debate on the budget affords me an opportunity to bring to the attention of this house the serious situation which is now threatening the stability and welfare of the entire dairy industry. Matters of grave concern have now *reached a crucial point, and for that reason it is urgent that a review be made of the position of this industry which is so important in our Canadian economy.
In this same debate a year ago I pointed out dangers threatening the prosperity of this industry, which since that time have contributed to a situation which demands prompt action on the part of the government.
Dairying is one of the most important industries in Canada, and provides two million Canadians with either all or part of their livelihood. This number includes those who are engaged in production, processing and distribution, as well as supplying equipment and various services. Of the farm population in Canada, 450,000 farmers are dependent on receipts from the dairy industry as a source of income. It contributes more than $600 million to our national commerce. A large area of Canada is peculiarly suited to this form of farming. On many of these farms dairying is the only type of f arming that will provide sufficient cash income to maintain families. If the dairy industry is not prosperous, then these farms will be abandoned. Many of these farmers are in districts some distance from other milk markets, which limits their production to either cheese or butter.
Not only is it an important branch of agriculture, but it is an industry which is important to mixed farming. Conservation of soil is dependent to a large degree on a healthy dairy and livestock industry. The upkeep of dairy herds is one of the most important factors in soil conservation and fertility maintenance.
There is a great lack of understanding between the consumer public and those engaged in the industry. It is a year-round business providing considerable employment for hired labour and a cash return throughout the year. It is not generally realized that


it requires years of labour to build up a good dairy herd, and long hours of work to secure high production. It is an expensive proposition, as the purchase price of a good dairy stock and upkeep of barns and silos requires considerable outlay of cash. It is an industry of long hours, as cows must be tended and milked twice daily through seven days in the week, and there is added to this work the care of milk in order that it may reach the market in a satisfactory condition. When prices are high, consumers are more conscious of food prices, and there is an inclination on their part to blame rising costs on the farmers.
Some seem to forget that the dairy farmer begins his work early in the morning and finishes late at night for six days, with another four hours on Sunday. On the basis of a 12-hour day-and many farmers work over this time-with four hours additional on Sunday, the total amount of time adds up approximately to a 75-hour week. There is no arrangement made for overtime in this industry. These actual facts as to food costs and the price received by farmers for their products should be considered. Dairy farmers to the number of 450,000, together with their families, and all the people from whom they buy, consume large amounts of manufactured products. If the income of this large group is so reduced that their buying power is impaired, it will have a marked effect on the manufacturing industry.
A comparison of prices between the years 1939 and 1951 is interesting. In 1939 it took the average man 15-6 minutes of labour to buy one quart of milk. In 1951 it took only 10-1 minutes of labour. On the basis of 100 in August 1939, the index of consumer prices of milk products was 125-4 in October 1941; of meat and eggs, 130-6, and of all foods, 124-1. In the latter part of 1951 milk products stood at 213-4, meat and eggs, 354-9, and all foods, 251-5. It is to be noted that dairy foods have not increased in price proportionately. At the same time the cost of labour to the dairy farmer increased 181 per cent from 1941 to 1951, and in that period his own food costs were 82 per cent higher. Dairy farmers are now in a position where they have to compete with industry for labour.
In the same period the average farm price for 100 pounds of milk increased 78 per cent. The cow population has declined 2-4 per cent, and the Canadian population has increased 21-6 per cent in ten years. During the same ten years the per capita consumption of milk has fallen 18 per cent in Canada, notwithstanding the fact that the protein value of two quarts of milk equals that of a pound of choice beef at a much lower price.

Prices of other commodities have climbed in the spiral of inflation. It is admitted that the dairy farmer is receiving more for his products than he did ten years ago, yet the increase received has not kept pace with increased costs. Farm labour wages, higher food costs, maintenance of herd and buildings, competition from cheap vegetable oils, and the general increase in the cost of living, have added to his difficulties. Better public relations between consumer and producer would do much to create a better understanding.
Importation of vegetable oils into Canada has threatened the dairy industry on an increasing scale in the past three years. This is borne out by the following table of importation of vegetable oils into Canada:

I am not entering into a controversy on the merits of these products', but I present these figures for the purpose of showing the competition which faces the dairy industry through the manufacture and sale of edible oil produced in Canada. These imported oils produced by cheap labour have replaced about one-quarter of what was once the dairy farmer's butter market. It is reported that "filled fluid milk" with the cream replaced by imported oils could be expected to find a place on the Ontario market soon.
There are other factors which have brought the present situation in the dairy industry to the point where it constitutes a national emergency. There is grave uncertainty among
The Budget-Mr. Blair dairy producers. This applies particularly to the cheese branch of the industry. The industry itself has had no control over the forces which have caused the present situation, which certainly was not of its own making. The factors which enter into the present situation are: First, the outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease in Saskatchewan early in this year; second, the loss of the United Kingdom markets, which has been our traditional market for cheese ever since confederation; third, the quota imposed by the United States which has shut off further Canadian cheese exports there and has led New Zealand exporters to enter the Canadian market; fourth, the importation of large quantities of cheese from New Zealand.
The outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease will result in more dairy cows being kept on the farms, and hence larger quantities of milk will be placed on the market. For years there has been a market for Canadian milk cows, especially young heifers, in the United States. During the periods when prices for milk products were low many farmers added to their income in an excellent market by producing a certain number of milch cows for export. Owing to the outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease there can be no further export of dairy cows to the United States until we are clear of the disease and the embargo which resulted therefrom is lifted. The unfortunate further outbreak of this disease clearly indicates that the embargo will certainly not be lifted during this dairy season. These animals retained on Canadian farms will add to the amount of milk on the market. Not only will this apply to the cheese producers, but the price structure of other milk groups will be in danger if surplus milk is backed up into their market.
Last year Canada produced about 16,400 million pounds of milk. It is estimated that this year there will be an increase of 250 to 300 million pounds. This increase would amount to the equivalent of 29 million pounds of cheese or 14 million pounds of butter. The national dairy council estimates that the problem of marketing may cause 500 million pounds of milk to back up on the Canadian market. When this surplus milk comes on the market, much of it will be manufactured into butter and cheese. The government has taken butter, but so far has not stated where the surplus cheese will be sold. More milk production will mean more dairy products produced in all branches of the industry with no outside markets to take care of the surplus.
It will be difficult to handle all this milk which would normally go to cheese plants in the flush production season. Cheese factories have been closing all over the country in

The Budget-Mr. Blair the past few years and there are indications now that many more factories will not open this season. There is a shortage of trained cheese factory and creamery operators, and farm labour has become a serious problem. There must be some outlet for the sale of the surplus milk which will be produced during the coming season.
The loss of the United Kingdom markets has been a serious blow. This has been our traditional market for Cheddar cheese for sixty years. At one time we exported over 200 million pounds of cheese to Britain, but in the last year our exports have been cut down to 29 million. During both wars the industry was encouraged to produce to capacity. It had no knowledge that this longtime market would collapse. Without export markets for our cheese products it seems absurd that New Zealand cheese was imported into this country after it had become apparent that the cheese was not needed here and would cause distress on the Canadian markets.
The loss of the United States market by the quota imposed has prevented further Canadian cheese exports to that country. If the Canadian producer cannot avail himself of outside markets, the amount of New Zealand cheese which enters Canada will not only interfere with our marketing program, but will seriously demoralize the whole industry. Much of the cheese imported from New Zealand had originally been intended for the United States market to earn dollars for New Zealand. When the United States placed a quota on further cheese imports, it became available on the open market, and a considerable quantity was purchased by Canadian firms.
On April 21 of this year, as reported on page 1427 of Hansard, I asked the following question on the orders of the day and received the following answer:

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Agriculture. Will he make a statement on the assistance to be given to the cheese producing industry? Will the assistance given to them bring the price in line with that of the concentrated milk producers who are at present receiving $3.30 on local sales?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Gardiner (Minister of Agriculture) :
maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I think it has been decided in the courts
that questions having to do with the price of milk are under the jurisdiction of the provincial governments. The question of cheese and milk in general has, I think, been fairly well taken care of by the government of Ontario. As to cheese production and' other related problems, they are dealt with accordingly.
On April 22, in answer to a similar question, the Minister of Agriculture stated:
There is a floor under butter of course, and as I said yesterday, there is a legalized position in Ontario in relation to cheese. Since most of the cheese is made in Ontario, the cheese position is well governed by that.

It would appear from the minister's answer that the onus for support prices or otherwise has been thrown on the government of the province of Ontario. Even there the marketing scheme could not toe expected to handle the present confused situation. I might point out that other provinces than Ontario are interested in the dairy industry.
The Minister of Agriculture has announced that the government is prepared to stand a loss of $6 million to support hog prices. In view of this statement there can be no reason for not supporting cheese. I have looked up the Milk Control Act, Revised Statutes of Ontario, 1950, chapter 233, and I find that the interpretation section contains the following:
(k) "milk" includes cream and such products of milk or cream as are manufactured or processed in any form, other than butter and cheese.
(m) "Processor" means a person engaged in the business of processing milk or manufacturing milk products, other than butter and cheese.
The Milk Control Act was amended in 1951 toy Bill No. 129, an act to amend the Milk Control Act. Section 3 of the amending legislation reads as follows:
Subsection 1 of section 5 of the Milk Control Act is amended by adding thereto the following clause: (hh) after a public hearing, prescribe maximum prices at which milk may be sold by retail in any market.
The words "other than butter and cheese" are to be noted. The question of a support program for agricultural products in this country is and has been recognized as a federal responsibility. For the Minister of Agriculture to endeavour to shift the responsibility to any province at this time is not consistent with his position on the question in the past nor with the policy of the government of which he is a member. I well recall, as does every other member of the house, the ringing phrases of the Minister of Agriculture when he assured Canadian farmers that a floor had been established below which prices would not be allowed to fall.
The situation today constitutes an emergency, the root causes of which are not confined to the dairy industry. If the cheese production branch is unable to market their product at a satisfactory price, then the whole industry will be affected. Something must be done to secure a market for surplus cheese at a fair price. Any loss in price will not only affect our dairy farmers but will have an effect on the whole Canadian economy. A satisfactory floor price below which prices will not be allowed to fall, thereby virtually destroying this essential industry, must toe assured to producers now.
Even this is only a partial answer. There must as well be an all-out sales effort by

the dairy trade and the government. Not only is a satisfactory floor price necessary, but some means must be found to dispose of surplus production. Failure to do so will give rise to a feeling of uncertainty which cannot help but spread to other related industries and in turn will reflect itself in unemployment in this country resulting from a lack of orders for farm machinery and other manufactured products.
I suggest further that the government again make representations to the United States government about the quota placed against imports of Canadian cheese, and the relationship this virtual embargo bears to our mutual agreement under the Geneva trade agreements. I for one have supported legislation to expand international trade, but if the application of escape clauses by other countries, who are also signatories to the Geneva agreement on tariffs and trade, is to continue to discriminate against Canadian producers, then I believe an obligation rests upon parliament to reappraise our position under this mutual agreement to expand trade.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with great interest to the speech which has just been delivered by the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Blair). I certainly agree with him that the dairy industry in Canada is facing an emergency. Very little cheese is produced in the prairie provinces, but being a person interested in agriculture and the national good I cannot help but feel that the cheese industry has a just case and that the government should consider the steps that the hon. member has suggested.
The hon. member suggested that further representations might be made by Canada to the United States, and that if action was not obtained from the United States, parliament should perhaps reappraise its attitude toward the Geneva trade agreements. I do not know whether the hon. member is suggesting that Canada might take retaliatory action, but I hope the government will not take such action, because the erection of one embargo followed by a counter-embargo would probably lead to a series of embargoes between Canada and the United States, with serious consequences to our economy.
I think the government might explore the possibility of obtaining a market for cheese in the United Kingdom. We all know that the United Kingdom is short of Canadian dollars and that that is why they are unable to purchase our cheese at the present time. At various times in the past we in this group have suggested barter arrangements. The
The Budget-Mr. Argue government has always turned a deaf ear to such suggestions. I am thinking now of the farm machinery inquiry by a legislative committee that took place in Regina. The committee found that farm machinery prices of companies producing in Canada and companies from whom we get supplies but producing in the United States were very high indeed. It seems to me that Canada might well sell cheese to Great Britain on the understanding that the funds obtained from cheese would be used for the purchase of British agricultural machinery. A considerable quantity of British agricultural machinery is being used in the prairie provinces at the present time. I can say that it has worked quite satisfactorily on most farms and under most conditions.
The hon. member for Lanark suggested a floor price under cheese. If the government is prepared to place a floor price under such commodities as eggs, pork and beef, then I for one certainly feel that the cheese industry has an equal claim to a floor price. In establishing any such floor price I would hope that the government would set a price that would in fact pay the producer a reasonable price for his cheese and ensure that the cheese producer does in fact receive the floor price. We have floor prices now, but they are floor prices in name only. The packers by paying less than the floor price have made a sham of the government's floor prices. For example, the floor price under eggs is 38 cents a dozen, grade A large, going into storage in any part of Canada. In addition to the 38 cents, the government stands prepared to pay up to 5 cents to cover the cost of storage.
So the packers buying eggs obtain from the government a net price of 38 cents per dozen because the government will pay the storage costs.
The floor price of grade A large eggs to the packers in the city of Regina, for example, is 38 cents a dozen. When I was home at Easter our farmers were not getting 38 cents a dozen. Of course we could not expect all the eggs to be grade A large, nor would we expect the floor price to be that high. But farmers were not even getting 30 cents a dozen. On the average the price the farm wife is receiving for eggs in my part of Canada is 14 cents a dozen.
I would not have believed that such low prices could exist when the government was supposed to have established floor prices if I had not seen the actual receipts. In fairness I should point out that the 14 cents is for the average eggs produced, but those eggs were fresh and probably three-quarters

The Budget-Mr. Argue would be grade A large. That price of 14 cents a dozen to the farmers is nothing less than an insult, and will certainly force those egg producers right out of business.
The so-called floor price under pork is not too much better. The price has been established at $26 a hundredweight for grade A carcasses basis Toronto. That is supposed to provide a floor in Saskatchewan of $24.50 for grade A hogs. The packers in Saskatchewan are not paying that floor price but something close to it for grade A and B-l hogs; but all the farmers of my constituency are living in either the buffer zone or the quarantine zone established because of the outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease, and their market is severely curtailed. The market at Regina takes only the cattle and hogs that can be slaughtered and consumed within the quarantine area. People in the buffer zone have to take their hogs to the Moose Jaw market. That market is jammed; there is a long waiting list, and the farmers cannot market their hogs when they are at a weight to qualify as grade A or B-l.
The prices paid to a particular farmer in my constituency by Canada Packers at Moose Jaw for grade A were $25 in one instance and $24 in another. Prices for B-l hogs in one instance were $24 and in the other $23.60. On one of these slips there is a heavy hog. It was graded as a sow. Technically speaking it was not a sow at all; it was a female hog that was overweight. It had never raised a litter of pigs, so technically speaking it was not a sow but a gilt, and should have been graded in the heavy class. Here was a perfectly good hog from which will be obtained perfectly good pork, but the farmer received a price of $13.75 a hundredweight, rail grade. The government is prepared^ to accept canned pork at 63 cents a pound in cans. I will bet my bottom dollar that most of the hogs graded as heavies and sows, for which the farmer receives 14 cents a pound, will wind up in cains and the packers will receive 63 cents a pound for that pork, making a handsome profit.
So I say the government should establish an adequate floor price for cheese, but the government should also take steps to enforce existing floor prices. I would say the government should provide under the law that packers must pay the established floor price, and if a packing company refuses to do so it should be haled before the courts and fined accordingly. Without such a provision the packing companies are making a complete sham of the government's floor prices.
The government has announced a floor price under beef of $25 a hundredweight for


good steers at Toronto. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) has told us that after freight is deducted that will give a floor price of $22.80 for choice steers at Saskatoon.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Not choice steers-good steers.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I accept the correction-good steers at Saskatoon. The floor price is not being extended to other grades of cattle, and the minister has advised farmers to keep their cattle on the farm, with the exception of those in good condition. Well, the cattle produced in my part of the country do not usually grade as choice or good steers. They usually grade as feeder steers, as cows or calves or something else. So the floor price under beef cannot possibly apply to more than a small percentage of the cattle normally marketed in my part of the country.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The floor price is not under beef; it is under cattle.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is live cattle, and if I was giving the impression it was dressed weight I accept the correction. I am quite certain that the price of $22.80 per hundredweight at Saskatoon will result in a price a good deal lower than 20 cents a pound for animals shipped to market in Saskatchewan. That is my opinion, and we will soon find out whether or not I am right. In the light of the experience we have had with floor prices under eggs and under pork, I just do not believe the farmer is going to receive $22.80 a hundredweight at Saskatoon for good steers, even though such a floor price has been announced. I hope I am mistaken; but if the farmer gets that price it will be the first time any floor price under livestock or dairy products has been provided directly to the farmer.
Together with other members of the house, particularly those from Saskatchewan, I was sorry indeed to learn of the fresh outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease in Saskatchewan. It occurred at a farm only five or six miles from my own farm. I do not know the names of the people concerned; I have not seen their names in the press, but I know the area very well; it is a beef-producing area where there are lots of cattle. It has been said that the outbreaks around Regina were in areas where few cattle are produced. In the area where the new outbreak has occurred large numbers of cattle are produced, not by large ranchers but because almost every farmer has from ten to twenty head of beef cattle on his own farm, while some have upwards of a hundred head. Right alongside the place where the recent outbreak occurred lies the Key West Excel P.F.R.A. pasture that normally takes some 2,500 head

of cattle. I would say that perhaps 150 to 200 farmers make use of that pasture each year by placing in it 10, 15 or 20 head of cattle. The farmers in that area are producing beef cattle and they are depending upon the P.F.R.A. pasture on which to turn their livestock out in the summertime. They just do not have the pasture at home to take care of their cattle during the summer. A neighbour of mine has 60 head of cattle; he has 60 acres of pasture. It takes from 15 to 20 acres of pasture per head during the summer months. He therefore has at home one acre of pasture for each head of cattle. The community pasture cannot be opened until this disease is finally cleaned up; but that 60 acres of pasture that this farmer has is under water because we had a substantial run-off this spring. When I left the west last week his cattle were out in the stubble fields, as were the livestock of most of the other farmers in that area.
This matter of pasture is a real problem. I do not know how it is going to be met. If the P.F.R.A. pasture is not opened, I shall be surprised if feed does not have to be shipped into that area. Because of the fact that the P.F.R.A. pasture has been closed, those farmers are going to suffer increased expenditures because of having to provide feed for their cattle throughout the summer months. On the orders of the day a couple of days ago I asked the Minister of Agriculture whether the government would consider giving any compensation to farmers in that area who were thus affected. But when we in this group, during the present session, have asked for such compensation, we have received a negative reply, and along with it we have usually had a few smiles from a number of cabinet ministers. They seem to think that if compensation is extended to farmers other than those who have their animals slaughtered, the door is going to be opened and there will be no end to the amount of compensation that will have to be paid.
I feel, however, that an exception to that stand should be taken with regard to those farmers who live in the quarantine and the buffer zones. Certainly those farmers in my locality who are depending upon the P.F.R.A. pasture should have from the federal government assistance to provide necessary feed supplies through the summer months. I therefore appeal once again to the government to consider that aspect of the matter, to survey the situation, and, if the problem is as I have stated it, to come to the assistance of those farmers until such time as the P.F.R.A. pasture is reopened.
The Budget-Mr. Argue
I had risen this afternoon to make a few remarks on the budget, but after listening to the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Blair) I thought I should mention something about floor prices, and in particular I thought I should say that I agree with his suggestion that a floor price be placed under cheese.
A great deal has already been said about the budget, and I am sure that anything I say will not be new. It seems to me that there are two main criticisms that can be levelled at the present budget. One is with regard to the statement of the Minister of Finance, (Mr. Abbott) when he introduced the budget, that taxes were being lowered. Along with the tables he placed on Hansard at page 1254, he forgot to place a table showing the income tax actually paid in 1951. If he had placed such a column on the record one would have then seen that instead of there being a decrease in the income taxes the effect of the budget is to increase by 6 per cent income tax for those in the lower brackets; that is, the amount of income tax paid, apart from the social security tax, in the year 1952 will be approximately 6 per cent higher than that paid in the year 1951. Without that explanation or without that table being placed in the budget, I say that the Minister of Finance was attempting to hoodwink the taxpayers of Canada. When taxpayers have paid all of their 1952 taxes they are going to learn that income taxes for 1952, as compared with those for 1951, have not been decreased by 6 per cent, as the minister stated, but rather have in fact been increased by approximately 6 per cent.
We in this group were particularly disappointed that the government did not follow the wish of the house and remove the 4 per cent provision with respect to medical expenses allowed for income tax deduction purposes. It was clearly the unanimous wish of parliament that the Minister of Finance allow all medical expenses as a deduction from income for taxation purposes. When the minister did not follow the unanimous wish expressed by this house he was thereby, in my opinion, making a mockery of parliament. According to their vote on the resolution presented by the hon, member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), members of all parties in the house believe that all medical expenses should be deducted from income for taxation purposes. I believe the government should have followed the wish of parliament instead of having made a mockery of the members' wishes as expressed in that vote.
Last night the member for Moose Jaw stated that the government should endeavour in a
1598	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Argue number of ways to make substantial savings with respect to expenditures. He has a right, as any other member of our group has, to his own opinions, and has a right to express them. As to some of the savings that he advocated, I agree with him. As to some of the other savings he advocated, I disagree with him. In fairness I think it should be pointed out that of the $315 million total that he arrived at as the total which the government might save with respect to expenditures, seventy per cent of it, or $225 million, was a suggested saving in the Department of National Defence. Judging by the speeches I have heard from a number of members in this house and the comments I have heard outside the house, it may well be that the government could reduce the expenditures of the Department of National Defence 10 per cent and, by squeezing out inefficiency, get the same defence effort that is now being obtained.
The suggestion of the hon. member that a means test should in any way be applied to the old age pension or the family allowance is something with which I cannot agree. I do not believe the means test should be reapplied to the old age pension, no matter how generous that new means test may be. Hon. members know that the Prime Minister of Canada has reached the age of seventy, and is eligible for and is receiving the no-means-test old age pension. The Prime Minister of Canada is on an equal footing with every other Canadian resident aged seventy when it comes to receiving the old age pension. Because the Prime Minister and every other person who has been in Canada for twenty years and is seventy years of age are receiving that pension, the stigma of taking it has been removed.
I would not like to see a means test reapplied to the old age pension, because then you give some people the opportunity to say: "Oh, I am wealthy; I am making a lot of money; I can look after myself; I do not need the old age pension." And other people, because of circumstances, must apply for an old age pension, and when they receive the pension there is a stigma attached to it.
Likewise I do not want to see the means test applied to the family allowance. When I was first elected to the House of Commons a taxpayer with children who did not receive the family allowance was given a greater exemption in filing his income tax return than a parent who received the family allowance. The government then proposed to allow a smaller exemption for all taxpayers who had children of family allowance age. That meant that everyone in Canada with dependent children received family allowances, and was not allowed to claim a greater exemption for dependents because family allowance was not


accepted. The very wealthy took the family allowance cheques, and then the government took back through income tax a large part or all of or perhaps more than they received in family allowance. In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, that is the way old age pensions and family allowances should be paid. They should be paid to Canadian citizens as of right. And then for the wealthy the government should tax back a large part of those payments in income tax.
At various times I have suggested certain increases in expenditures, such as suggested in the resolution dealing with family allowance standing on the order paper in my name. I suppose if members advocate increases in government expenditures they might suggest to the government some ways in which the government might increase its own income to cover those expenditures. I was interested to read in the U.S. News and World Report of April 18, 1952, that corporation taxes in the United States are very much higher than corporation taxes in Canada. This article points out that corporation taxes of Canada amount to 50 per cent, or slightly more, of corporate profits, whereas corporation taxes in the United States are on the average about 60 per cent. In other words, corporate taxes in the United States are 20 per cent higher than they are in Canada. There, in my opinion, is where the government can get more than $200 million annually in additional revenue.
I believe there is a sound argument in Canada for a capital gains tax. Many people buy speculative stocks and shares, and over the last few years have made enormous profits that are not subject to income tax. I feel that a capital gains tax could well be applied to such gains, and the government could make good use of the additional revenue in providing for increased social security expenditures.
There is only one other subject that I wish to mention at this time. I see my time is running out; therefore I shall be able to make only a brief reference to it.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Thank you. I want to reply to the speech made by the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) in the house on Wednesday, April 12. In replying to a former speech of mine on the collection of income tax from farmers, the Minister of National Revenue had this to say, as reported on page 362 of Hansard:
However, it is not my purpose to quarrel with the various figures which have been presented, but rather to disagree emphatically with the conclusions which have been drawn from those figures.

In other words, the Minister of National Revenue accepted the accuracy of all of the statistics that I had placed on Hansard. I worked out a lot of these statistics in longhand, and I was afraid I might have made an error in one place or another. The minister says that these statistics are accurate enough. He goes on to say:
Criticism based on averages can be very misleading.
That was the point he was trying to make throughout his speech-that while the statistics I used were correct, my conclusions from those averages were wrong. In attempting to prove that my conclusions were wrong, the minister had this to say-I might say, the minister was attempting at that point to build up an argument as to why the amount of income tax paid by farmers in Quebec and Ontario is not as large as the amount of income tax paid by the farmers in western Canada. The minister said this:
In the first place the occupied farm land and the average area per farm is substantially greater in the prairie provinces than in eastern Canada.
The minister said that no one should use averages, because if he does he will come to wrong conclusions, and then he starts using averages himself. He goes on to say:
Furthermore, the average size of farms in the prairie provinces is from two and one-half to three and one-half times as large as those in Ontario and points east.
Once again the minister himself was using averages. But of course the minister should realize that the amount of income tax paid by a farmer has nothing whatever to do with the size of the farm itself. What counts is the net income resulting from the farmer's operations, and 50 acres of good productive agricultural land in the Niagara peninsula of Ontario will probably provide a farmer with a larger net income than 1,000 acres of grazing land in the constituency that I represent. Therefore, if one farmer's holdings are twenty times as large as some other farmer's holdings, that in itself has nothing to do with the relative amount of income tax the farmer pays.
I have some further statistics' to give the minister that I think prove that there is discrimination between the collections of farm income tax made in western Canada and in eastern Canada. I should like to quote again from the minister's speech at page 362. The minister says:
It may or may not be a fact that the taxation division is getting proportionately more of the tax actually payable from western farmers than from eastern farmers.
The Budget-Mr. Argue
The minister says he does not know; it may be the case; it may not be the case. Then he makes this statement at page 363, referring to eastern Canada:
The proportionately larger staffs are considered to be justified because the task of finding the comparatively few farmers who are actually taxable in an area such as Quebec is more difficult than in the west, and it is also more difficult to determine the actual income on which the tax should be based.
He says he does not know whether there is a larger proportion of the tax being paid in Ontario and Quebec than in western Canada, but admits it is more difficult to collect in Ontario and Quebec. Then he adds this:
In the more prosperous farming areas in the west the number of products dealt in is generally smaller, the majority of sales are made in large amounts mainly at one season of the year, and records of many of these sales are readily available.
The minister says, on the one hand, that he does not know whether the farmers of western Canada are paying a larger proportion of the tax than in Ontario and Quebec, but then goes on to say that it is easy to get at the farmers of the west, and that therefore it is no wonder that the tax collectors are doing a much more efficient job out west.
Well, if it is harder to get the tax in Ontario, one would expect that there would be relatively more assessors, based on the number of farmers, in this province. In other words, an assessor, one would expect, would have to look after less farmers in Ontario than an assessor would in say Manitoba, where it is easy to collect the tax from the farmer. Yet, while in Manitoba there is one inspector for every 1,520 farmers, in Ontario there is one for every 1,756 farmers. The minister stated that it is harder to assess the farmers in Ontario, that more work is involved, and that in many instances the records are not available. Yet the average income tax assessor in Ontario must deal with 236 more farmers than the average assessor in Manitoba.
While the income tax assessors did not find many farmers in Quebec from whom they obtained income tax, nevertheless the ones they did find paid reasonable taxes. The average income tax paid by taxable farmers in Quebec was $255 while the average in Saskatchewan was $331, and that in Manitoba was $242, or somewhat less than the Quebec average. There is a good deal more efficiency in over-all collections in Manitoba than there is in Quebec, because the average income tax collected in Manitoba was $242, while that in Quebec was $255.
Let us see how successful income tax inspectors were in Saskatchewan, on the

The Budget-Mr. Argue average. In that province there were 74 income tax inspectors in 1949 and 20,000 taxable returns were made. In other words each inspector was able to find 271 farmers who paid income tax. In Manitoba each income tax assessor obtained 183 farmers who paid income tax. In Quebec there are 23 assessors, each one of whom, in a whole year's work, found only nine farmers who were charged income tax. It took the income tax assessor in Quebec 52 weeks to find nine farmers, or one for every six weeks' work. I wonder what he was doing? Certainly he must have been asleep on the job. Yet, there are lucrative taxes to be collected in Quebec because the ones they did find paid $255, on an average. Each tax assessor in Quebec obtained taxes from farmers to the amount of $2,216 during the whole year. The salaries paid by the Department of National Revenue are, I venture to say, well over $3,000 a year. In addition to salary, travelling expenses incurred by income tax assessors are paid by the government. I am sure therefore that for the 23 income tax assessors the department has in Quebec the government spent $2 in 1949 for each $1 obtained from farmers by way of income tax.
The department asked 30,000 farmers to send in income tax returns, and the minister reported that only 14,000 complied with the request. But what about the other 16,000? Anyone in Saskatchewan who receives a letter from the income tax branch had better file his return right away, or someone will be out to see him. Why did not at least 95 per cent of those who were asked to file returns comply with that request? Perhaps the 14,000 said, "Well, we can afford to send in returns because we know we do not have any income tax to pay", while the ether 16,000, who might have had tax to pay, said, "We will not bother, because probably they will not ask us again."
On the average, each income tax assessor in Manitoba collected $44,000 by way of farm income tax in 1949: The average for each assessor in Quebec was $2,216. I suggest that the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) should do some transferring in his department. Our income tax inspectors in the west are good inspectors. They are efficient, they are doing their job and they are collecting a lot of income tax. On the other hand the ones in Quebec are an absolute failure, and those in Ontario are a near failure. I suggest therefore that the minister should send some of the Ontario inspectors out west, where most farmers now pay income tax whether they are asked to do so or not. He should send some of the Quebec inspectors out west, so that the income tax people out there could give them

some training. They could then be sent back to the east and, in those circumstances, I am sure the government would find that its income tax returns from farmers in the central provinces would improve considerably.
I am a farmer, and while I believe that farmers should be given certain further exemptions than are now provided, I do say that, as applies to other groups, once a law is established farmers should be required by government officials to comply with that law. I believe farmers in Quebec and Ontario are just as honest and as upright as those in any other part of Canada; but if income tax inspectors are falling down on their job, then I do not think we can blame the farmers if they do not shell out voluntarily. So I suggest to the Minister of National Revenue-
