maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, rising to take part in the debate, before entering upon the subject matter I intend to discuss I should like to make some few comments on what was said by the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Blair).
Hon. members who come from western Canada have been told many times that, by accepting the wheat agreement, we have acted like socialists, that we have gone too far, and that we should go back and put grain on the open market. Today we have been given a good example of exactly what has happened in Ontario. At one time cheese, from the standpoint of marketing, was in the same position as wheat. However the cheese producers preferred to be independent of the government, to withhold cheese from the operations of any government department, and run the industry themselves. What did they do? Well, to make a long story short, they priced themselves out of the market.
It is time the farmers in the dairying industry in Ontario got together, and indicated their willingness to come, with hat in hand, and say, "We made a mistake, and we are willing to go back where we were before". I am sure that if they do that they will get some reward. It may not be just what they think they should get, but certainly they will be recognized. I know that there is no one in this country who has more feeling for the farmer in any part of Canada than the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner).
I want to say a few words about the budget. I have never spoken on the budget before, but as far as I can see this is a good, sound budget. It does three things.

First, it has given us a sound dollar. The whole world is looking to Canada today, but that was not so two years ago. At that time our dollar was down to 90 cents, but now it is up. The great United States with its millions of people-150 million to 180 million, we do not know just how many exactly-is doing its utmost to produce and make its dollar worth as much as possible. In Canada we have 14 million people only but we have a sound dollar that today is even better than the United States dollar.
I want to say something about my constituency and a little about the constituency next to mine. We heard a wonderful speech the other day by the hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Weaver) who painted a great picture of his constituency and tried to give the people of eastern Canada some idea of what it actually is. He tried to indicate the great wealth there is up there, and I am sure that everyone realizes just what that means to Canada.
For a few minutes I am going to try to draw a similar picture in connection with my own constituency which runs alongside his. My constituency is 560 miles long and about 84 miles wide. We split the town of Flin Flon. There are 1,200 of my constituents who live in Flin Flon. I am going to try to give hon. members some idea of the country from Wollaston lake down to where agriculture starts. Some of the ministers have flown over this lake.
This great lake, which is close to the Northwest Territories, contains great fishing grounds. The fish must be flown out to Flin Flon. Then next we have Reindeer lake, another great fishing ground. Here the fish are flown out in the summertime and brought out by caterpillars in the winter. These lakes are miles and miles north of what we call civilization, Reindeer lake being some 200 miles north of Flin Flon.
Then you come down to the great mining areas. I should like to indicate something of what has happened just south of Flin Flon where a large area is being opened up. The Hudson Bay Mining and Smelting Development Company have claims totalling 8,350 acres. No one knows the value of the minerals in those acres. No doubt a big development is going to occur in that country and no one can begin to imagine the wealth that will be taken out of there.
We are asking that some attention be given to the construction of a railroad from Lynn Lake, north to Reindeer and Wollaston lakes, then to Athabaska and down to Prince George. That is asking quite a lot but if it were done it would open up one of the greatest mining territories in the world.
The Budget-Mr. Ferrie
East and north of Reindeer lake is found what is called green stone, and then south of Athabaska you find red stone. The green stone area is where most of the minerals are found and that is where they do most of their surveying and exploration work. Last year I mentioned that the area around Athabaska was one of the greatest mining areas to be found. They are developing uranium and other minerals. On the Saskatchewan side of Flin Flon they have taken out minerals to the value of many millions of dollars. Then they started investigating and found that the slag heap contained $90 million worth of a new kind of ore, so now they are going down into the Saskatchewan mine again. They are going to empty all the shafts, reprocess the material, extract this valuable ore-they do not tell us what it is-and then put the slag back into the mine again. In the Hudson Bay Mining and Smelting Company mine 3,500 feet down at the bottom of a shaft they have cut a drift inwards and have built a room there half as large as this chamber. It is 3,500 feet under the ground. They say that there is enough ore down there to last, at the rate they are taking it out now, for the next twenty years.
The reason I raise this matter is that we have 12,000 people in that area and they have no road leading westward. They have to travel east sixty miles to The Pas and then 150 miles south before they can go west. The Saskatchewan government have been asked to build a road from Nipawin to Flin Flon, and have said in the provincial legislature many times that it is up to the dominion government to build this road. But they have not asked the dominion government to build the road. They have not done anything about it. All they have done is to talk about it in the legislature in Regina. By no stretch of the imagination have they come to the point where they have said how much it would cost, how much they would be willing to pay themselves, and how much they wanted the dominion government to contribute.
I think this attitude is very unfair to the people who live in that northern area. They are entitled to a road running westward, and it is up to the provincial government of Saskatchewan to help those people to be able to travel westward. It is only fair and reasonable that the provincial government should do this. I would not mention this matter if it were not for the fact that it affects the people of my constituency. I have been trying to help them to get a road but the Saskatchewan minister of highways does not seem to want to help

The Budget-Mr. Ferrie these people who pay taxes and produce wealth for the province of Saskatchewan and also for the dominion.
I have told the house now about the fishing in the northern part of my constituency and the mining a few hundred miles farther south. Now I come to the region around Hudson Bay Junction where there is lumbering. The lumberman is having quite a hard time. As hon. members know, we have had a lot of trouble so far as lumbering in that district is concerned. The lumbermen and trappers around Hudson bay have had a pretty hard time during the past winter. I have not heard much kicking on their part, but they want things done in the proper way. They want a chance to go into the bush and produce a living for themselves, something that they cannot do at this time.
Farther south in my constituency we have an agricultural area which is one of the greatest agricultural regions in Canada. The development of the Carrot river delta is just beginning. I should like to say here that the hard work of the hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Weaver) has certainly been helpful. He has been able to get the Manitoba government to make representations to the federal government, and the federal government has utilized the P.F.R.A. to help to start the development of that part of the country. The hon. member for Churchill told the house yesterday that in this delta there are about 2,500,000 acres within his riding. The delta region runs [DOT]right across the Manitoba boundary into Saskatchewan between the Saskatchewan river and the Carrot river. In that area there is some of the finest agricultural land that there is any place in the world.
Last winter we drove in a motorcade from Carrot river to The Pas. We travelled by an old bush trail down to the river and drove fifteen miles up the river to the boundary between Saskatchewan and Manitoba. There were about fifty or sixty cars, and at the boundary all the people got out and had lunch at that spot. This part of the prairie is a wonderful piece of land. All it needs is draining. All it needs is a few million dollars to be spent on it, about $10 an acre, to make it a really productive area. I understand that Manitoba has made an agreement with the federal government with respect to the development of that part c, the delta within Manitoba. Why does the Saskatchewan minister of agriculture not do the same thing for the part of the area within his province? Saskatchewan will never be able to develop it. They will never be able to spend the money. There is one point to which they stick. They would rather let
[Mr. Ferried
the area go undeveloped than do away with the system of lease agreements. They want to lease the land instead of letting people homestead it or buy it. If they would turn the matter over to the federal Department of Agriculture, in a few years the P.F.R.A. administration would have at least 1,500,000 acres in the province of Saskatchewan producing. There would be a lot of good people in that part of the country and a lot of good business being carried on.
It is a shame to leave it the way it is now. It is a mess and some day they will have to pay for it. I hope that something will be done in the near future because we need development of that region. As the hon. member for Churchill told the house, there is about 20 to 40 feet of solid silt that has come down from the mountains and elsewhere on the prairies over a period of thousands of years and has settled there. It is a detriment to Canada that this land is not producing today. Where you see willows 3, 4, 5 and 6 inches through you know very well that there is something in that land and that it should be producing for the benefit of the people of Canada.
Before I leave that area, many times I have heard it said in this house and by people from eastern Canada that the Hudson Bay railway is always in the red. That is not a fair statement. I am sure the people here do not really understand the situation. The Hudson Bay railway starts about five miles north of The Pas, and from there up to Churchill it carries its own load. It does not belong to the C.N.R., as we always thought; it belongs to the government. The strangest thing about it is that the government has no rolling stock, so when they take something up to Churchill they have to rent the rolling stock. If they were to take that division and add Sherridon and Flin Flon, making it one division north of The Pas, I do not think it would ever be in the red again; it would always be in the black. They took the Temiscouata railway and added it to the C.N.R. The Canadian National was willing to take that line, and I do not see why the Canadian National should not take over the road from The Pas to Churchill. Then if there is any deficit the whole country meets it. I do not see why we should have to stand by and watch this part of the railway going into the red all the time. That is not right. All the development that has taken place in that north country could not have been undertaken but for the fact that this railroad was built north to Churchill. Many of us thought more lines should have been built, which would have led to even greater development, but no doubt that will come later. However, I think it is time the C.N.R.

realized that that is a part of the Canadian railway system which should be taken over and put in the black instead of the red.
Now I want to say a word in regard to a defence highway from Winnipeg to Edmonton. I spoke about this two years ago, and I am still of the opinion that something ought to be done about it. We are spending millions of dollars on radar equipment for the north; yet if we had to take a big gun from Winnipeg to Edmonton it could not be done under any circumstances. We have had one of the driest springs in many years, but even so, our best roads running through that country are very bad. The defence department should realize that the people on the prairies are entitled to some protection. They say there is no chance of an enemy coming from the north, that we will not be hurt that way. Well, if I were a minister I do not think I would agree with that. Look at Edmonton; then look at New York, Montreal and Toronto. You will see what a short distance it is by plane between those points. Edmonton has everything that might be needed for an army-oil, food for the troops, and lots of room to be able to watch all around. Once more I am asking that some consideration be given a highway from Winnipeg to Edmonton to help in the defence of western Canada.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Why not go right through to the coast over the Yellowhead route, following the pipeline?

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That is up to you fellows. That would not protect us at all, though I would be satisfied with the Yellowhead route.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I want to say a few words in regard to the speech made last night by the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatcher). It matters little what was in his mind, but what he said was serious to those of us from western Canada who have fought for so many years to help the man who was not able to get a pension because he had the odd quarter section of land that perhaps was not producing anything and was not an awful lot of good to him, but which he did not want to turn over to the government. Some men were independent. They said, "All right; I will get along," and they got along on $4, $5 or $8 a month. I know one man over 70 who had a cow. You can hardly believe it, but he used to live the whole year on the milk he got from that cow, because he would not let them file a lien against his homestead. He had lost everything in one way or another. He was old and sick, and was not able to farm properly on his quarter section of land. We fought to have pensions given to people like that; and I want to say to the hon. member for Moose
The Budget-Mr. Ferrie Jaw that for what he said last evening he is absolutely a disgrace to Saskatchewan.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order. I think the hon. member will realize that he should modify the expression he has just used in reference to the hon. member for Moose Jaw. I do not think he would want to say of any colleague that he was a disgrace to any part of Canada.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: All right, Mr. Speaker; I will withdraw the statement. Perhaps I can put it in more flowery words and at the same time bring the facts home to him. He is young. He may be politically unwise, as one of his colleagues said. After all these years of hard fighting that we have done to get this matter into the position in which it now is, he may be able to think that we should say we should go back to a means test.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, if the hon. member will permit me to make an explanation-

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: -I should like to say that I certainly did not suggest that we should go back to the kind of means test we had previously. I should like to correct the hon. member. What I said was that I did not think it was sensible that the taxpayers of Canada should be paying a pension to people with incomes of $5,000, $6,000 or more a year. I am sure that the farmers that my hon. friend has spoken about would not come in that category.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is still a means test.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I take the hon. member's explanation; but as far as he is concerned, it is absolutely impossible to segregate those to whom it would apply and those to whom it would not.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Why?

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: If you are going to have a means test, you are going to have a means test; and that is all there is to it.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: But there is a great deal of difference between the means test which we had previously and the one I suggested last night.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
You cannot have what my hon. friend suggests, and he knows it. I am not sure whether he was on that committee or not. In any event, he has heard many times that the application of the means test was to anybody and everybody; and that is all you can have. You cannot segregate those to

The Budget-Mr. Ferrie whom it will and will not apply; you cannot say you are going to have the means test apply to this man and not to that one. You have got to have the means test apply to all, to see whether they have that specified amount of money or whether they are receiving that specified salary. It is an absolute impossibility to have a means test unless you go back to where we were before; and we are certainly not going to do that.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I hope not.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Then there is another thing. The hon. member talked about savings. What do the savings mean? The hon. member made a statement about various savings. As far as he is concerned, the savings just meant that we were not going to get the services. That is all they meant. The hon. member for Moose Jaw said: All right, save; stop the services; stop Canada. Yet our great Saskatchewan is going ahead and is going to produce and produce. We are going to bring the wealth into the country. As the hon. member for Churchill told the house yesterday, there is great wealth in the north. In the great prairies wheat is being produced. We had 500 million bushels last year, as it was thought, and now we come to the point where there is 700 million bushels. We hear talk about the millions and billions that we are going to spend. We are not spending them foolishly. Do you want protection? As I told the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Stewart), he wanted to have his porridge and eat it. That is what the hon. member for Moose Jaw wants. He wants to have his porridge and eat it. He wants to make a fuss over what? He tries to make it over a few million dollars. What does the expenditure of a few million dollars mean? A few million dollars expenditure means the services to the people of Canada.
Coming down here from Saskatchewan, I was talking to a conductor and he said that one of the finest things that had ever happened to Canada was the surplus that we have; and that is a fact. We have that surplus. We are paying off the debt. I want to say this to the hon. member for Moose Jaw. If he had an 8 per cent surplus in his business, would he for one minute think that he was doing a good job? That is all you have got here with a great government that handles millions and billions of dollars. Surely we are today in a position to cut down our public debt and to render the services that are necessary to the people of Canada; and then, in the final analysis, we can say that we are ready, if the time comes that we should have to do so-and we pray God that we shall never have to-to put out money to help to keep the country going. If we come
[Mr. Ferried

to a depression, we are in a better position because we had surpluses; and a good businessman knows that.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at this stage in the budget debate I can readily come to the conclusion, after listening to the many speeches, that the members of the opposition groups are against the budget. As we have sized up the reaction from across the country, it seems also that there is a good deal of criticism in the regions beyond the confines of this chamber.
I have been vitally interested in the debate because it is my first budget debate, and budgets concern themselves with one of the basic functions of parliament, the collection and the spending of public money. I found the evening of April 8 a most interesting and entertaining one. We had a sense of the dramatic present in the chamber on that evening, a situation which does not prevail too frequently in the House of Commons. We had the galleries filled with tense and expectant taxpayers. I found the performance of the Minister of Finance to be quite an interesting one, almost up to the calibre of a Shakespearian actor. Since that time we have had such comments as a sleight-of-hand performance, Hallowe'en pranks, and the accusation of the use of a false face, the typical mask of the stage.
I have been intrigued with government spending for some years now, even before I came to this chamber. I have found myself somewhat bewildered by the astronomical proportions this spending was reaching, particularly in the post-war era. I assumed that on coming to the House of Commons I might gain a better knowledge of why all this money was necessary, where it all comes from, and where it all goes. From the comments I have heard thus far in the house, however, I am coming to the conclusion that after the debate is finished I shall still be asking those questions as to why it is all necessary and where it has all gone. For example, there is the fluctuating surplus that we have before us this year. It began as an estimated amount of, I think, $30 million; it grew, in certain newspaper reports, to something like $900 million; and finally, in the statement of the minister, it emerged as just a little over $300 million.
The other big item in the budget, the matter of defence spending, is of course going to be exceedingly difficult to pursue. It was my privilege to join the committee on defence spending just yesterday, and I can see that there is a real Sherlock Holmes problem involved in keeping track of, or gathering

information on, the devious ways of this huge amount of $2 billion for the purpose of defence preparations.
To get down to the main themes that have emerged in the discussion, they seem to be those of extravagant spending, and excessive taxation. Those are the two points emphasized in the amendment brought forward by the members of this party. I am sure that, in regard to the first-that of extravagant government spending-there has been considerable disappointment. For a time, with election rumours in the 'air, it was hoped that we might be favoured with a "sunshine budget" this year. There was hopeful optimism that we would see substantial cuts and economies; but as I listened to the presentation of the Minister of Finance I found that any suggestion of economy was strangely lacking in his speech. The conclusions seemed to be that any relief from the high level of taxation, and any reduction in government spending, must come from a reduction in the burden of defence expenditure, or else a steady increase in the wealth and incomes of the people, which would tend to make government spending and taxation seem relatively less heavy.
Hopeful optimism of this kind of course is to be expected from the taxpayer. Being realistic about the matter, if we had exercised sufficient foresight, I think we could have come to the conclusion that there actually could be, under the present government policy, no reduction in spending or in taxation. Increasing government expenditures are inevitable under a policy of expanding government control, power and influence. We all know that governments on all levels have tended to increase the degree of control in the affairs of the nation. From long experience, too, from the evidence of history, for example, we know that governments from time immemorial have been notoriously spendthrifts. Wherever they enlarge their activities it is to be expected that the cost of administration must go up. It is a sort of "easy come, easy go" proposition. As a matter of fact, it was this difficulty that first led to the establishment of the principle of no taxation without representation, one of the basic fundamental ideas behind responsible government.
We know, too, that political machines are costly and expensive; the larger they grow the greater the expense; the longer in office a party remains, again the greater the expense tends to be. Fortunately Canada has been free from major financial scandals such as those that emerge from time to time out of the complexities of the United States government, but perhaps that is due more to accidental circumstances than to higher moral
The Budget-Mr. Dinsdale standards. We are a smaller country and we can keep closer control of things; and the people, at least up until recent times through their parliamentary representatives, have been able to keep a fairly close watch on the treasury.
Under these circumstances we cannot expect that government spending and taxation will decrease. We find that, in the minister's presentation, the blame for increasing costs and spending, taxation and so forth, was placed upon the rise in social welfare expenditures and the increasing cost of our defence program. The hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatcher) made reference to this last night in his remarks. He has already received honourable and dishonourable mention on several occasions since, so that I am going to be comparatively kind in the observations I am going to make on his speech. I was most interested in his presentation last night. He did point out where other economies might be effected to the extent, as we already well know, of $315 million in departments other than defence and social welfare, as well as an additional amount of $225 million in defence spending. A presentation of that kind will require detailed analysis, but no doubt amongst the suggestions that were put forward-and those suggestions were put forward in response to a direct challenge as to where economies might be effected-will be found some that are worth while. He has been criticized for attacking the present basis of our universal old age pension. He is quite capable of defending himself, and I do not have to continue on that point. But we are all of the opinion-as was indicated by the vote last fall-that the social welfare programs of t'he kind represented by the universal old age pension are necessary in the kind of world in which we live today.
Social welfare programs of necessity increased rapidly during the depression, and ever since the depression have expanded rapidly. In fact, it was the impact of the depression that gave the impetus to the idea of the social welfare state. The social welfare state is not entirely all good, nor is it entirely all bad. It is not a panacea. I think there are some very excellent points in its favour, and there are some very dangerous features in the notion of the welfare state. For example, it is possible that the huge expenditures that are involved in maintaining an expensive social welfare program can be used for political expediency. Under these circumstances it makes it very difficult to carry on successfully our form of democratic government, because the group responsible for the administration of these huge expenditures, by subtle insinuation, can

The Budget-Mr. Dinsdale suggest that these benefits are due to government largess. That has been a feature in the United States, and to a certain extent in Canada.
It is obvious that government functions are increasing. Services are increasing. The central government is assuming tasks, functions and responsibilities that were formerly performed by the family, by the church, by local governments and neighbourhood communities. This is all a part of the trend that is under way to more and more influence, power and control exercised by the central government.
As I have already indicated, it means considerable expense to the taxpayer. I would remind the house that this is but one solution to the social problems that emerged out of the depression, and it is not necessarily the only solution. I do not think that increasing government control is necessarily the final and absolute solution of all the problems that are facing our way of life and our civilization. Actually, you know, real social security cannot be bought. You cannot measure social security in terms of dollars and cents, as we tend to do. Actually, there is a tendency to confuse social security and financial security. If we look at the problem of the older citizens in our society-and his numbers have been increasing as the result of the increasing longevity due to medical science, better health services and so forth-we realize that the basic pension of $40 a month is not going to solve the real problems of our older citizens. I happen to be interested in such movements as Twilight clubs and other organizations that are trying to deal with the real problem of social security, that of giving our older citizens a meaningful place in society. The $40 a month is going to be of very little use to them, of very little value, if, as at present, they are forced to a large extent to live alone in a garret unwept, unhonoured and unsung, waiting for the grim reaper to come along with the proverbial scythe.
They want more than that. They want a meaningful place in society. Unfortunately, with the speed of modern industry and the demands of industrial life, they tend to become misplaced as a worker at a relatively early period in life, and this just at a time when they are beginning to enjoy a longer life span.
That problem is not going to be solved by minimum incomes of $40 a month. Those incomes are very important; but our responsibility to our older citizens will have to go much farther than this if we are really going to give them their proper place in society today. I do not believe that central governments, governments at the federal level, are


in a position to provide that type of social security. This is a problem that must be worked out by local communities. It is a problem the neighbourhood must work out. It is a problem that must be handled in the close face-to-face contacts of human relationships. This might be the time to start to consider the possibility of handling social problems by educational programs which encourage a solution at the individual and local level, rather than by an increased dependence on the super-state. So long as we move in the direction of state control we are going to find that government will become more expensive and, as a result, taxation will have to be imposed to meet ever growing demands.
I might have mentioned the work going on in the field of industrial relations. An entirely new experiment in human relations is taking place in modern industry, where there has been a great deal of bitterness and a great deal of dissatisfaction because the worker, like our older citizen, had lost his meaningful place. With the industrial revolution he became a part of the mechanized assembly line. The job he was doing did not make much sense, and did not have much meaning or purpose for him. The result has been that industry has been plagued by strikes and disturbances of various kinds.
We now discover that when the human factor is taken into consideration in industry, the problems between management and workers are considerably alleviated and softened. I have in mind the famous experiments conducted in the Hawthorne factory of the Western Electric Company, just outside Chicago, by Elton Mago one of the pioneers in the field of industrial relations. A very simple fact was demonstrated in a rather dramatic way. A special experimental group was gathered together and subjected to varied conditions of work-changed working hours, changed rates of pay, a five-day week-and so on. They were given all those other things peculiar to industry today; and it was found that, regardless of what was done, production continued to increase. Finally the experimenters reverted to the original conditions. They sorted out the X-quantity, which was the simple fact that, because of the special attention received, this experimental group had found a new meaning and purpose in the job they were doing, and as a result produced at the higher levels.
These are some of the major difficulties being faced by our industrial society. At the present time the only thing we have done, acting automatically and unconsciously, and following the line of least resistance, has been to-endeavour to solve these problems by state

control, government control, and by increasing government participation at all levels of life-family, industrial, business and what have you, with the inevitable results that are being criticized here today.
It is more expensive. It means excessive taxation even to the extent that taxation begins to interfere with individual initiative, and the productivity of business corporations as well as that of individual workers. All this has been glossed over, and an attempt has been made to justify the situation by the fact that Canada is enjoying an unprecedented period of prosperity. We have constant references to the fact that Canada is passing through prosperity such as she has never enjoyed before. The parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sinclair) made reference to this the other day, upon which occasion he quoted certain United States authorities that were somewhat impressed by the economic state of affairs in Canada at the present time.
Of course there have been other references to Canada that have come out of the United States. We will recall that one American senator suggested that the United States might well annex Canada. For all we know, the laudatory references referred to by the parliamentary assistant might have been only a subtle continuation of this policy to win Canada into the American fold by flattery. I do not know.
The hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Sin-nott) also made reference to the level of prosperity Canada is enjoying, and justified the trend toward increasing government control in that fashion. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) visited my constituency last week and, in a speech reported in the Brandon Sun for last Friday-I believe the date is April 18-made certain statements which were given this heading: "Present Prosperity of Canada Due To Government Policies." The news item goes on to say:
Hon. Stuart Garson, Minister of Justice, said in an address here-
That is, Brandon.
-Thursday that Canada's present prosperity results not from a favourable world atmosphere but from policies instituted by the Canadian government in conjunction with the governments of the United States, Great Britain and some European countries.
Well, now, what is the real explanation of Canada's prosperity? Actually we were quite unprepared for it following the war. Most economists-there were one or two who were right-basing their forecasts on what followed after world war I, were prepared for a recession, if not a depression, following world war II. The monetary policies adopted at that time reflected the gloomy forebodings of the economists. They were prepared to meet
The Budget-Mr. Dinsdale the impact of the anticipated depression or recession. But it never emerged. The monetary policies then established tended to contribute to and to aggravate the difficulty we have been having with inflation during the last two years.
Actually, very few of us had realized the tremendous changes that had occurred in connection with the world's economy as a result of the upheaval of world war II. We were still thinking in terms of the depression because Canada was still in its throes. We were only slowly emerging out of the depression in 1939. I should like to pose some questions. Where would Canada's prosperity be if we had lost the war? I am sure that the responsibility for the successful conclusion of world war II was more that of the armed forces than the result of any machinations of any government body. I hope we remember that when we come to discuss amendments to the War Veterans Allowance Act.
If the war had never occurred, what level of prosperity would Canada have been enjoying today? I have indicated that the war actually awakened Canada from her depression lethargy. The balance of economic power as well as political influence changed to a large extent from the old world to the new and Canada automatically fell heir to the results of this transition without any great effort on her part. It was a process that took place as a result of the devastating effects of a global war.
Where would our prosperity be if we were not favoured geographically as we are? Where would it be if we had not the natural resources that we are only now beginning to exploit? And a final question: Where would it be without the continued high level of United States capital investment in the exploitation of these resources? I have a statement here-unfortunately I have not the reference-which I should like to place on the record. It reads:
Foreign capital pouring into Canada has saved us from some most unpleasant consequences. Without this inflow we would have been getting dangerously short of credit in the United States and elsewhere. We would have been in a worse predicament even than four years ago when we had to curb buying and travelling in the United States and generally pull in our belts.
That crisis was brought on by buying far more from Uncle Sam than we were selling him. The same has been true in our trading of the last 12 months. Though our exports took rather an unexpected splurge in December, nevertheless we finished the year almost $125 millions behind. This deficit covered trade with all countries but the difference with the United States was most important. And in other international items, too, we were in the red, items such as net tourist travel, freight shipments, etc. All the figures are not in yet, but when they are our total deficit on current international account may be the largest ever.

The Budget-Mr. Dinsdale
Luckily for us, while we have been doing this extra shopping and travelling in the United States, shrewd Americans have been investing their dollars in our oil, iron ore, power, chemical and other resources. That's what has kept our credit sound. That's the reason our dollar is on top of the heap."
On April 23 the United States ambassador made a speech in Montreal, which was reported as follows:
Stanley Woodward, U.S. ambassador to Canada, today defended investment of U.S. capital in Quebec and said "denunciation of foreign capital trusts and unions have become a commonplace tactic" in this province only in recent years.
And again:
"Natural resources must be exploited if they are to be resources instead of buried treasure," he said.
"To do so requires large amounts of capital, technical knowledge, and a willingness to gamble on the outcome of often unprofitable explorations.
I think you will agree that my fellow countrymen have helped Quebec in these respects, and have contributed to the notable rise in the French-Canadian standard of living."
We are aware that there is considerable United States investment in Canada, particularly in connection with the development of our natural resources. This investment has played a large part in bringing about the present level of Canadian prosperity.
I have mentioned before that the prairie provinces do not believe in this myth of prosperity. We cannot believe in the myth of prosperity because of our population losses. We are a relatively depressed area. We have been losing population to the more favoured central provinces. Why should we be impressed with the prosperity that exists in Ontario and Quebec, when actually it is a relative thing so far as Canada as a whole is concerned?
We must consider the national viewpoint in this regard. As is well known by hon. members, Manitoba is faced with the loss of two representatives in the House of Commons because of the harsh necessities of redistribution. Our voice is going to be weaker rather than stronger as we endeavour to grapple with the complex problems of government. There has been no move on the part of the "have" provinces to assist the "have-not" provinces. In this regard the old doctrine of an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth unfortunately has been followed. You can understand then why we are not necessarily enthusiastic about this picture of overwhelming prosperity that is referred to from time to time.
There was one project in Manitoba that was assuming worth-while proportions as a tourist attraction. I refer to the international peace garden on the boundary between Manitoba and North Dakota. This project

has been stymied this year by the withdrawal of the federal grant of $15,000 just when it was becoming a profitable source of tourist dollars. Here we seem to have economy in reverse. I was surprised, as were other hon. members who are interested in this worthy project, and as were citizens right across the country, when this grant was withdrawn, especially when $50,000 is being provided for the United Nations doors or, to carry it to extreme, when $10,000 is being granted to an organization to promote a thrift campaign. I am sure that the spontaneous representations that have been made on behalf of this worthy project are sufficient indication to the members of the government of the feelings of the people right across Canada about this shortsightedness.
My time is running out. I was going to deal with one specific problem faced by the prairie provinces, but this matter was dealt with adequately by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) this afternoon. I refer to farm income taxation. As I move around my constituency my attention is continually drawn to this problem. Ever since the matter was brought before the house last fall, as well as during the spring session of 1951, the farmer has become aware of the discrimination that exists. The explanations given have not been quite adequate so far as he is concerned. Saturday Night of January 26, 1952, contained an article which has brought forth some inquiries. I should like to quote one or two paragraphs as I think they will help to present an objective viewpoint of this matter. They read:
In 1949-the latest year for which you can get figures-23 employees of the income tax department collected an average of $255 from 200 farmers in the province of Quebec. There were in Quebec, according to the 1941 census, 134,000 "farmers and stockraisers." In the same year in Saskatchewan 74 income tax officials collected an average of $331 from 20,000 farmers. There were in Saskatchewan, according to the 1946 prairie census, 115,000 farmers. In Ontario, 92 officials collected an average of $242 from 8,010 farmers. There were in Ontario, according to the 1941 census, 161,600 "farmers and stockraisers" . . .
On the face of it, the collection of taxes from the farm population is highly inequitable in Canada; and those who are so minded attribute the inequality to the basest possible motives.
We have had an explanation of the situation in terms of the comparative difficulty of determining farm incomes in Ontario, and particularly in Quebec, with their smaller units; but these explanations have not entirely satisfied farmers on the prairies. One solution that has been put forward this afternoon is to increase the intensity of activity or interchange the personnel so that more effective administration of income tax affairs

can be carried out in those areas which at the moment seemingly are not being adequately covered.
I have been dealing largely with government extravagance, and the other side of the picture of course follows axiomatically. If you are spending lots of money you have got to collect lots of money notwithstanding the fact that the suggestion is often put forward that all these benefits are due to government largess. You have got to tax and tax heavily to realize the income necessary to meet the increased services of government. Today we are taxing to the extent of almost one-third of our national income. The distribution of the tax dollar between Ottawa, the provinces and the municipalities is something like 49 cents for Ottawa and 51 cents to meet the combined obligations of the provincial governments and the municipalities. With one-third of the national income drained off in federal taxation there has been a great deal of discussion concerning the prevailing state of affairs. We have heard protests from corporations which have put forward presentations that the level of taxation is resulting in a loss of productivity and producing a situation which can prove actually harmful to business development and activity in Canada.
But even the ordinary taxpayer is beginning to feel the pinch. As he moves toward greater dependence upon the state, he is beginning to feel that there is a price to pay, and protests are rising right across the country. We are becoming aware too that government spending is not sacrosanct. It contributes to inflationary effects as does excessive private spending. The problem seems to be that the government is not aware of the outcry. We get no clue that it is at least from the presentation of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott). The major difficulty is that the sinner cannot see his sin. There is no repentance possible when there is no awareness of sin. It reminds me of the situation of the chap who had been a bit of a reprobate during his lifetime. His clergyman was trying to get him to repent as he neared the end. He said to the chap, "Do you renounce the devil and all his works?" The fellow replied very feebly and weakly that he did not think this was a time to be making bad friends of anybody. Maybe that is the explanation of government policy. If we were closer to an election than we think we are perhaps we would come to that conclusion. There is the situation as I see it. I have no difficulty at all in supporting the amendment submitted by the members of this group.

speechtext:
The Budget-Mr. Huffman policy, and says that budgeting lor a $9 million surplus this year will only mean a difference of $21 million, so that this year we will have a surplus of $881 million. In one place he subtracts; in another he adds; in another he takes percentages when it is to the advantage of the speech he is making. If he wanted to be fair I should think he would use percentages in relation to the surplus. If you relate the $9 million surplus that has been budgeted for this year to the $30 million which was budgeted for last year, you will find that is three and one third times greater than the other. If you divide $902 million by that figure it will give you the sizeable surplus of around $300 million.
Then at page 1577 the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Hees) had this to say:
-there is not the slightest doubt that we will end up this year with a surplus at least as great as the one we had at the end of the year just past.
For a long time this government has been trying to convince the opposition that the policies it has adopted have been in the best interests of our people. How has that been done? Some have called the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) the super-optimist, the crystal gazer or the seer; but if you look back over the reports he has given this house from time to time you will find that they were honest reports of what he considered would take place within this country. It was not a case of being a crystal gazer; it was a case of taking the best available information. In this country we have an excellent bureau of statistics, which gathers facts from all over the world. They are able to give us the anticipated national production and the anticipated gross national income. In addition to the bureau of statistics, Canada has trade commissions in practically all the countries with which we are doing business, and I was very pleased to note that only last week three new trade commissions were opened in countries with which we had been doing some business but with which we hope to do a much greater volume of business. So it was not a case of crystal gazing; it was a case of placing facts before the house, and those facts have been among the best barometers this country has had. As far as I can ascertain, the reports the minister has presented in the house from time to time are the only thing conservative about him. Always at the conclusion of the fiscal year the gross national production and the gross national income have been higher than he indicated they would be.
Now I would like to say a word about production in this country. Unfortunately at the present time we have an outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease in Saskatchewan, tMr. Huffman.]
which has closed the natural outlet for our livestock products. As a result we cannot dispose of those products in the natural market, and the producers are suffering some hardship. I sincerely hope this difficulty will soon be overcome. I would like to suggest to the government one thing I believe is in our own interests, and which would help overcome such a situation as we face at present. There is no question but that our basic metals find a ready market today. The products of our forests also find a ready sale in foreign markets. I believe we should have more industry which would use our basic metals and forest products, thus providing for a greater popu-. lation which would consume our agricultural products. In that way we would avoid the surpluses of food we have at the present time. I realize that we cannot reach perfection immediately, but we are attempting to do what is in the best interests of all the people of Canada.
Speaking of opportunity within Canada, I note that the hon. member for Eglinton gave this quotation:
My father made your yoke heavy and I will add to your yoke-
On the same page he also quoted:
Cease to do evil, learn to do well.
The government of Canada is attempting to provide opportunities for the people of this country. Then it is up to the people of our country to accept the yoke of responsibility. I am certain that our people and those that have come from other countries, with the background that they have had, will certainly accept that yoke of responsibility and will go on and continue to make a greater and better Canada than we have at this time. The hon. member has stated that we should cease to do evil and seek to do well. I think we should continue on in the pattern we are going.

speechtext:
I think it is always interesting that an absolutely honest report be placed before the people of Canada. I should like to congratulate the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) on the report he gave on March 14, which appears at page 440 of Hansard. I should like to quote his remarks in part:
This is a convenient point at which to mention that the Department of Trade and Commerce has just completed its annual survey of investment intentions for the year 1952. Total private and public

investment is likely to be of the order of $5 billion, involving an increase of just under 10 per cent over the total of $4-6 billion for 1951 which was itself a record year.
And this is the part which I think was absolutely fair to the people:
Perhaps half of the increase over 1951 will represent physical volume and half higher prices.
This again just points to the fact that the 'bureau of statistics possibly realizes, as has been indicated in our papers just recently, that there is an increase in the price of steel of $3 a ton, and that fact cannot help affecting the economy within this country. We are developing steel within this country to a greater extent from day to day; but while we have to look to other countries to supply us with that commodity, we shall have to pay the price they ask. I therefore say that this is an honest report to the people of Canada when it says that one half represents physical volume and the other half represents higher prices.
As to this surplus that has been indicated here from time to time, there is always a question that has occurred to me, namely, when is a surplus not a surplus, In the province of Ontario from which I come I have noted that the premier and provincial treasurer was extremely happy to relate that he had a substantial surplus at the end of his fiscal year. I can truthfully say that when the government of Ontario went to the people of that province for a mandate, that certainly was. one feature that was spoken of as being a characteristic of good government. If it is an indication of good government in a province for it to have a surplus it should be an indication of good government in the federal field. In Ontario the error in estimating revenue was 16 per cent, while the federal Minister of Finance was in error only 8 per cent in estimating his revenue. In other words, Canada had an additional 8 per cent more revenue than was budgeted for while the province of Ontario has, 16 per cent more. What I should like to know is where is a surplus not regarded as a surplus. Within the province of Ontario it is taken as an indication of good government. I am certain that in this house the leaders of the same party could well commend the government of Canada for that surplus that has been provided rather than -try to discredit it at all times.
The two members that I have mentioned- the hon. member for Broadview and the hon. member for Eglinton-are now indicating that possibly at the end of this coming fiscal year this government will have a surplus; the size that has been indicated by the 55704-102J
The Budget-Mr. Huffman figures given by the hon. member for Eglinton is $881 million. To me this is indicating to the people of Canada and to the world at large that we have a sound financial position in Canada to which the outside world is looking with envy, and which our own people as well are most happy to go along with.
For a few minutes I should like to refer to the "Report of the Postmaster General for the year ended March 31, 1951". Here is one place that I think a bit of the surplus might well be used. In looking over this report- and this is the 100th anniversary of accepting from the British government the mail responsibility in Canada-I note that on page 19, under the heading of transportation, it is stated:
During the year $13,672,978 was spent on land mail services other than railway, an increase of $770,000 over the previous year; $13,985,713 on railway operations, an increase of $5,118,692 . . .
I realize that the government had to make with the railway companies a contract to carry the mail, but that proportion of increase is not comparable to the service that is provided by the land mail services of the Post Office Department. The amount that has been indicated of $770,000 is a small and insignificant increase, when we consider that there is a group of 14,000 rural mail couriers who, six days out of the week, are bringing the mails to approximately two million people and who provide an excellent service. I would recommend to the government that something be done for these people.
We find that many of these rural mail couriers have a handicap but they provide an excellent service. Under the present system, when their contract comes up for renewal, they are afraid to tender at a price that is comparable to the services they give, for fear that someone else may tender below them and they would lose that livelihood which they have obtained through the contract for some period of years. I think it is most unfortunate, with the type of contract that we have at the present time, that those people who have oftentimes provided 15 or 20 years of services are just not able to get the contract they should have. I would recommend to the government that a committee be set up to study all phases of this act as it affects these people, who under all hazards of weather and road conditions provide one of our most excellent services, to one-seventh of our population. They are couriers of goodwill. I recommend most strongly that the members of this government do their utmost to see that these people are taken care of in the manner in which they should be. They have only the members of this house to recommend to the government what should be done. On the basis of this very report the

Private Bills
railways were increased by $5 million, or practically 30 per cent, and the couriers have not been taken care of. As I have indicated before, it is up to the people within this chamber to do what they can to support those who supply one of the most excellent services in a most excellent manner.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at eight o'clock.

Agreed.

The house in committee on Bill No. 61, respecting the British Northwestern Fire Insurance Company-Mr. Henry-Mr. Beaudoin in the chair.
Section 1 agreed to.
Preamble agreed to.
On the title.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Blair) presented the case of the dairy farmer most effectively to the house this afternoon. To those hon. members who did not hear him speak I commend a reading and digesting of his remarks in Hansard. They threw considerable light on the situation of our dairy farmers. Tonight I should like to take up a few minutes of the time of the house to deal with marketing and our trading situation, particularly as applied to agriculture.
I have just returned from the Easter recess, as have many other hon. members, and I attended a number of meetings and auction sales in my riding. I talked with a great number of farmers about the agricultural situation, particularly about markets. I regret to say that the situation is not too favourable today from the point of view of the farmers.
[Mr. MacDougall.l
I find that dairy cattle which formerly sold for from $300 to $350 are now selling at from $100 to $150 less than formerly. I find that the beef cattle situation is also in a turmoil. We trust that the recent floor price placed on cattle will eventually clarify the situation, but at the present that situation is not too good. I found also that small pigs which formerly sold for from $11 to $12 are now going begging at about half that price. I found also that poultry producers are facing a rather unusual situation as to the future.
We are approaching the productive season in agriculture with uncertainty, misgivings and doubt as to just what the future holds in store. I realize that it is always nice to be optimistic like the hon. member for Kent, Ont., (Mr. Huffman) who just preceded me and who was most optimistic as to the future. He referred to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) and regardless of what we may think of the minister at times, I think we all agree that he is always most optimistic as well. But we have to face the facts. While I rather hesitate painting a dark picture and being accused of being an apostle of gloom, nevertheless I feel sure that the facts I intend to place before the government will be accepted in the spirit in which they are presented.
I listened with great interest to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) when he presented his budget early this month. I was especially interested in his remarks about our export trade, particularly as it affected our primary products. I had thought that the distress signals which are flying would have brought some remarks from him as regards this phase of our national economy, but I was disappointed. I felt that they warranted some specific reference in the budget speech.
I studied the minister's speech in Hansard most carefully and I find that he made only a brief reference to export trade. He said that all was not well but that the Minister of Trade and Commerce along with himself had every hope that exports in 1952 would equal or better those in 1951. The minister's reference to our continued loss of export markets might have been more correct if he had said that it is true that some of these markets have been lost but the Minister of Trade and Commerce and himself believed that we will export more because we are exporting materials for which there is a great demand in many parts of the world. But these conclusions hold little hope for our agricultural producer. Today we have lost many of our important outlets for agricultural products and unless something is done immediately to rehabilitate our export markets situation things will be serious indeed.

I should like to give a few figures in connection with certain agricultural products which were formerly shipped to England. In 1938 we supplied 27-5 per cent of the total British imports of barley; this market was completely lost in 1951 to Russia, which is now the largest supplier. In 1938 we supplied 93-9 per cent of the total British imports of oats; in 1945 we supplied 96 per cent; but in
1948	we lost this market to the iron curtain countries and other sterling areas.
In 1938 we supplied 254,000 hundredweight or 24 per cent of the British imports of beans, but by 1951 we were not shipping a single bean to Great Britain. In 1945 we supplied 43 per cent of the total British imports of beef. We lost this market to the Argentine republic but found an alternative market in the United States. As we all know, that market has been shut off owing to the foot-and-mouth disease. This is a recent example of what can happen to such an alternative market.
In 1938 we supplied 18-1 per cent of the British imports of bacon. As every hon. member knows, Great Britain provided one of our largest markets for bacon. This market was built up continuously from 1940 until by 1945 we were supplying 83 per cent of the total British imports. In 1946 we supplied 73 per cent; in 1947 we supplied 74-4 per cent; in 1948 we supplied 70 per cent. In
1949	we started to lose this market to Dent-mark, Poland and The Netherlands. In 1951 Canada supplied only 16,000 hundredweight of total British imports of over 4,426,000 hundredweight. Of that amount, Poland supplied 730,000 hundredweight, The Netherlands supplied 695,000 hundredweight and Denmark 2,953,000 hundredweight as compared to the 16,000 hundredweight obtained from Canada. Our percentage of this market is now considerably below the pre-war level of 1938. With respect to ham, in 1938 we supplied 34 per cent of total British imports. This market was steadily built up until 1947 when we supplied 78 per cent of their total imports. Now that market is lost. The hon. member for Lanark pointed out very clearly to us this afternoon the situation so far as cheese is concerned. In 1938 we supplied 23 per cent of total British imports of cheese. This market was built Up until in 1945, for example, we sold 1 million hundredweight or 31 per cent of the total British imports. There has been a steady decline in sales of cheese in this market until in 1951 our exports were reduced to 234,000 hundredweight out of total British imports of 3,384,000 hundredweight.
The Budget-Mr. Catherwood Turning to poultry, during the 1940's Canada built up an export market for poultry in the United Kingdom. In 1947 we supplied 107,000 hundredweight or 18 per cent of their total imports. We have now lost this market and iron curtain countries such as Poland and Hungary have become the principal suppliers. With respect to eggs, in 1945 Canada supplied 56 per cent of total British imports of shell eggs and 26 per cent of their dried egg imports. In 1948 we supplied 79 per cent. Now that market is completely lost to Poland, China and other sterling countries. As to condensed milk, in 1938 Canada supplied 56 per cent of Great Britain's total market. Now that market is lost to The Netherlands and other sterling countries. Finally I come to apples. In 1938 Canada supplied 42 per cent of the total British market. That market too has now disappeared.
The above examples of these important segments of our Canadian trade have been checked with the trade and navigation accounts of the United Kingdom tabled in the British House of Commons so there is no doubt as to the authenticity of these statements. It can be reasonably argued that it was inevitable that sooner or later our exports of agricultural products would revert to the pre-war levels. However, these figures indicate that not only have the 1938 levels been lowered but we are facing the most serious financial and trade crisis in our history. With Canada being the only dollar member of the commonwealth, her markets have been practically erased altogether. Exports of the products I have named together with a number of others are below the 1938 levels, and of late we have noted that England is now reducing tobacco imports by 75 per cent. This will mean a very serious blow to Canadian tobacco producers.
The United States as an alternative market has certainly not been very promising. Canada, together with other nations, has endeavoured to have the United States rescind its ban on dairy imports which was applied under an amendment to their defence production act. As all hon. members know, this action was contrary to the international obligations assumed by the United States as well as Canada and other countries under the Geneva agreement on tariffs and trade. We must admit that our wartime level of trade or even a moderately reduced level is dependent upon whether Canada's post-war position is as favourable as it was in pre-war days. The serious problem confronting Canadian producers is not to maintain wartime levels of trade or even moderately reduced levels. The fact is our trade has
1616	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Catherwood fallen away below the level of 1933, and even this low level will be again seriously reduced in 1952.
When this serious threat has been brought to the attention of the government they have always pointed to the alternative markets in the United States. It is true the United States has been an excellent market for our Canadian farm products. History of trade has shown, however, that whenever the United States has a surplus and Canada has a surplus, and both countries are anxious to market the same product, the United States raises its tariffs or uses some other device to prevent our exports from entering that country. In that way they exclude our products from the United States. The stability of the United States market as an alternative export market for our primary products is very questionable for the following reasons: First, the congress amendment to their defence production act, which restricted the importation of cheese and other dairy products, seriously affected Canada. This action was protested not only by Canada but by New Zealand, Norway, Australia, Denmark, France, The Netherlands and Italy. It was an open violation of the Geneva general agreement on tariffs and trade.
Notwithstanding President Truman's message to the nation of January, 1952, recommending the repeal of this amendment, no action has been taken. The matter comes up for discussion again in June but it is very doubtful that the amendment will be rescinded prior to the election which is to take place in that country in the fall of this year. A second reason is that there is a bill now before the United States Senate, which was introduced in February of this year, asking congress to protect United States farmers against imports of Canadian feed grain. This comes at a time when Canada has a large crop of coarse grain to market and there are many millions of bushels of damaged wheat for which we require substantial export markets.
A third reason is the escape clause provisions in the United States trade agreement extension act of 1951. This presents an ever ready threat to the stability of our exports to that country. Therefore with these unstable alternative outlets in the United States in constant danger of being cut off we realize how important that matter of Canadian export trade is to us when we stop to think that one out of every four Canadians earn their livelihood in industries connected with the export trade. It is definitely a matter of great national importance.
The Progressive Conservative party has suggested in and out of the house on many


occasions that the government should initiate action requesting that a trade and economic conference be held to be attended by the economists and other experts of the commonwealth countries to study this matter. We have suggested the following reasons which I think are most important: (a) to review normal channels of trade between member countries now lost or seriously threatened;
(b)	extension of trade channels now existing;
(c)	consideration of action towards convertibility of currency; (d) a review of the effects of present blocked sterling practices and the possibility of their removal; (e) the possibility of Canada purchasing within the sterling bloc raw materials now secured elsewhere, at least to the degree that Canada might regain its traditional markets for primary products in commonwealth countries; (f) to explore the possibilities for Canadian enterprise in the amazing commonwealth investment and resources as a source of supply for raw materials required by Canadian industry.
Unfortunately the government did not see fit to take the action that has been recommended by my leader and other members of the Conservative party. I repeat that today the situation facing our farmers is made more difficult because of the loss of the alternative market in the United States as a result of the unfortunate outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease. In this regard 1 should like to ask the government if they have seriously com sidered every possibility and every angle of negotiations and arrangements with the United Kingdom government and the government of the United States whereby exports of meats now being shipped from New Zealand and Australia to Great Britain might be diverted to the United States and comparable quantities might be shipped from Canada to England. As all hon. members know, under United States laws, meat from a country where there is a disease-infected area is not allowed into that country. But their regulations do not preclude imports from Australia and New Zealand, so it seems to me that these difficulties could be overcome by some arrangement similar to that which was worked out among the United States, Great Britain and Canada in connection with aluminum.
Our loss of markets has brought about a situation that strikes at the very roots of the agricultural economy of Canada. Constructive action is required immediately. No one believes for a moment that the government can do everything; that would be impossible; but the farmers of Canada feel that the government should do something. I suggest that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), who is also Minister of Defence Production, dispatch his departmental officials

or better still go himself immediately to the United Kingdom with the proposal that Canada divert some millions of dollars in defence orders to the United Kingdom, which in turn would permit them to purchase our bacon, our wheat, our cheese, our apples and other primary products of which we have been the traditional suppliers.
In passing, Mr. Speaker, 1 do not think we should wait any longer for the Department of National Defence to make its decision on the question of arms standardization.
I trust the government will give these few suggestions very careful consideration. These are matters which concern all of us. They concern every member of parliament. We as representatives of the people express our views in good faith and trust the government will consider our representations in the same spirit. If this is done and we approach these problems from the standpoint of the common good, then the prestige of parliament will be greatly enhanced in so doing.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I am going to endeavour to express myself in the English language, and I immediately beseech the indulgence of my English-speaking colleagues if I do not have exactly the words to please their ears. I will do my best to say what I think ought to be said on the questions presently occupying the attention of this house. It is the duty of every hon. member to express the opinions of his constituents, and I think I would fail in my duty if I did not make a few remarks on the budget. I have heard a lot of things said and I am sure I will not say anything new on this subject. On the other hand I consider it is right for me to bring to the attention of different departments matters which to my mind should be looked into, especially on behalf of the small people whom I represent, since 95 per cent of my constituents are what I would call middle-class citizens.
As I said a moment ago, I have heard a lot of things said about this budget. First of all, emphasis was placed upon the fact that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) comes along and declares a surplus for this fiscal year of $350 million, in round figures. Some people on the opposite side of this chamber claim that if the predictions of the minister had been right the burden of taxes on the shoulders of our citizens would have been lessened. Well, I am of the opinion of the minister when he declares that it is not a big error on his part to make a mistake which works out at about 1J per cent of the gross revenue of over $3,500 million. Of course if these things could be foreseen there would
The Budget-Mr. Dupuis be no particular reason for any Minister of Finance to declare a surplus just for the pleasure of taxing. On the other hand it is really providential that this surplus has been declared. I am not a big financier, but I think it is a good policy to pay our debts in times of prosperity and not wait for times of depression. After all, with the heavy expenditures this government has to face at the present time, particularly in connection with defence, one is amazed that our debt not only does not increase but actually decreases, which is far better for the economy of this country.
Of course I would have liked nothing better than to hear the minister declare that all taxes would be reduced. But while he is a very capable minister, I do not think he is such a miracle man as to be able to go ahead and spend more and more all the time, yet be able to take off part of the taxes already paid by the citizens. My policy is to pay as we go. I think that is better for any government. From my point of view it is not a good policy to have future generations taxed for expenditures we are making today. And no one has ever contested the necessity of those expenditures, especially for defence, because we know very well that by preparing ourselves and preventing a war we are assuring peace. Even if we have to spend money and send troops overseas, that is a protection because, as I have heard here before, it is better to settle these affairs far away than have an enemy come to this country. It is better to invest our money in preparation than to be forced by lack of preparation to face a war which would be disastrous not only to other countries but to our own country as well.
We hear that taxes are too high. Well, of course everybody knows they are high, but that does not prevent our good citizens from the western part of this country coming along and asking for more expenditures; asking millions for their wheat, for instance, and for other expenses we are supposed to meet. That does not prevent them asking for millions and more millions for the western part of this country. I have no objection to helping settle some of the problems that may be of a national nature, but on the other hand I do not like to see those same people coming along and reproaching us for putting on taxes when a big part of those taxes are to pay what they are asking for their pari of the country.
