subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We have everything that counts.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Perhaps you have a monopoly on good administration, but it has not proven to be so in your province.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You are just foolish now.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If you think it is foolish, you can simply laugh at it. Any time the hon. member wants to meet me on any ground I shall be willing to answer him, but not tonight. I repeat that I am not a financier.
I am far from being a capitalist, as I know some on the other side of this chamber are.
I have always thought, however, that whenever your dollar was the best dollar on the monetary market, that meant good administration. Well, we did not hear any of the hon. members on the other side admitting the high position of our,foliar. They would not do it. There is a particular reason for that, and that is that they find it difficult to admit this government has done any good.
I am not going to say that everything this government has done has been good. I do not believe the government thinks that is so. But as I said when I first came into this house, when we judge a government or a party we put the good actions on one side of the balance and the bad actions on the other side. We weigh them, and when the good actions are heavier than the bad we vote for that government. That is what the people have done in past elections and that is what they are going to do in the coming election.
Is it not a sign of prosperity when money from foreign countries comes to Canada for investment? If that is not a sign of prosperity, then I know not a thing about finance. Let us take into account the high budgets of the provinces and the municipalities. Where does that money come from? Does it come simply from those provinces or from those municipalities? No, it is a reflection of the prosperity that is spreading right through this country. In 1939, Mr. Speaker, the province of Quebec had a budget of about $50 million -perhaps a little more or a little less, but let us call it $50 million. Now they have a budget of $200 million. Where does that come from? Simply by taxation? No; it comes simply by reason of the prosperity of the country, by reason of the increase in business. We hear all this criticism from the other side of the house. What is the use of all the time running down our country, and of always saying that this country is badly governed? Do you think that it will bring new industries here or will bring new investment capital by going ahead and making that kind of comment on the good actions that have been done by this government?
The Budget-Mr. Dupuis I think it is absolutely against the interests of our country not to place before the public and before other countries knowledge of the prosperity which has been the result of the direct action and the good policy of this Liberal government of which I am proud to be a part.
As to these provincial budgets and municipal budgets which amounted to $50 million in 1939 and which have risen to $200 million, some will say that that is inflation, All right. I do not know enough about inflation or deflation to speak on the subject, but I have lived in a situation which is much worse than inflation, from my point of view, and that was in a depression. I lived in a depression from 1930 to 1940. I was a member of the city council of Montreal and a member of the city executive. The relief costs in the city of Montreal alone were $1,500,000 per month. I would rather have a little bit of inflation than have that kind of depression. Was that under a Liberal government? No; it was under a Conservative government, under a leader who, when he was no longer prime minister, could think' of nothing better to do than go to England and invest his capital on the other side.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: With his top hat.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We have lived in depression times. With all the investment of new capital, with all the prosperity that we have seen in this country, with all our natural resources, we are sure of not living again in such depression times if the people of this country continue to place their confidence in the heads of the Liberal party.
Let us now study the budget, properly speaking. I am not going to deal with all the items; but I have heard so many bad things said about it that I feel I must mention some of the good things. First of all, in my speech last year I mentioned certain things. I am sure that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) did not allow those tax reductions simply because the member for St. Mary spoke. But on the other hand I realize that he gave what I and some other members asked for, namely, a reduction in taxes on frigidaires, washing machines, radio sets, automobiles, tires, soft drinks and other items. Those reductions will certainly help the family budget. Then in addition, when we passed legislation to abolish resale price maintenance, that was something that also helped the family budget. We can see the effect of it today, because today you can buy a frigidaire for from $150 to $175 less than the former price, taking into account the 15 per cent tax reduction recently announced. There is a reduction of some $75

The Budget-Mr. Dupuis on a washing machine. That is what I consider to be good administration. That is what I call taking into account the wishes of the people as expressed through their representatives. That is what I call a democratic government, ready to listen to whatever good requests are made to it.
My hon. friends on the other side of the house did not mention all the good things in this budget. There are, of course, some little things that I myself would have liked to see abolished. But on the other hand, I do not think you can expect perfection from a government. I am darn sure-that is the way I talk to my people when I meet them on the street-or very sure, perhaps I should say, that the representatives of the people here would have liked the government to listen to the suggestion made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) with respect to medical expenses. I myself would have liked to have that four per cent provision removed. But let us hope that this will be done in the near future. I am of the opinion that medical costs should be deductible from the amount taxable. Consider the situation of a man earning $4,000 a year. He pays some taxes. He pays for four years, five years or ten years-and it is only in order that he should do so-and he has no chance of getting any reimbursement. Whatever is left after payment of taxes, he just balances at the end of the year. Then one year he has bad luck, as I recall it, and he has $400 or $500 medical expenses to pay. There you are. He is up against it. He is in a bad situation. I hope this situation will be changed.
I am here to fulfil my duty, but that does not mean that I condemn the government with respect to everything. I am here to say what I think ought to be said. In my opinion this is one of the suggestions that ought to be listened to, and I hope it will be listened to in the near future. It is not only the member for St. Mary who speaks in this way. The other day in Le Canada, I read a comment of the correspondent for that paper. For those who do not know it, I may say that Le Canada is a Liberal paper in Montreal. I do not think that anybody who knows Le Canada will doubt that it is a Liberal paper. They said that some will be embarrassed by the amendment coming from the C.C.F. or the Social Credit group-I do not remember which it was-on the four per cent provision with respect to medical expenses. May I say that I am not at all embarrassed. After all, I am not going to vote against the government, in a vote of non-confidence, just simply because a couple of my points of view have not been accepted and when 98

per cent of the whole budget, under the present circumstances, is satisfactory and ought to be satisfactory to the whole of the people.
I really regret that the Minister of Finance has not seen his way clear to make a greater reduction in the tax on cigarettes. Bon. members of this house ought to know that if there is smuggling-and I am quite sure there is- a three-cent cut in the price of a package of cigarettes will not prevent it. I was under the impression that, in order to avoid all that smuggling, a package of cigarettes in this country should cost no more than 30 to 35 cents. Yet in our province anyway we are still paying 43 cents.
I have here an article published by the flue-cured tobacco marketing association of Ontario, in which it describes the smuggling of cigarettes as having reached unprecedented levels. It states, in #art:
"Few Canadians have any conception of the wide-open nature of this border," says the committee. "It is not only undefended, but as far as cigarette smuggling is concerned, it is also indefensible. Not only are there part-time customs stations which close at designated hours (usually after nightfall), but there are places where several trans-border roads lead through a town on either side of the main road manned by the customs."
The article closes in this way:
"Even now," the committee quotes a customs officer-
And a customs officer is a government employee who must know what he is talking about. He must know what he is up against when he is trying to do his duty.
"Even now," the committee quotes a customs officer, "we're too busy checking tourists to chase smugglers."
Citing the "Sherbrooke section" of the R.C.M.P. command as an example of a border hot spot the committee says that there are four or five smug routes into the section for every constable on the local establishment. "Even a cursory glance at a good map will show," says the committee, "that the unguarded roads and trails in the stretches between the ports are a much more obvious feature of the local landscape than the official customs points of entry."
The extent of smuggling is indicated by the number of people one sees every day smoking American cigarettes. I hope the Minister of Finance will be able to see his way clear to make a generous reduction in the cigarette tax. As I said earlier, I make these remarks, not by way of any real criticism of the government, but because it is my view that they should have looked after these two matters more properly. Let us hope that our wishes will come true in the near future.
I will vote against the amendment and the subamendment, because I am not going to support a vote of non-confidence in the government, and place myself alongside those whose ideas I do. not share. And I would give

some advice to my hon. friends in other parties: I am a Quebecer, a Montrealer, I know, of course, that those parties would like to have the support of the province of Quebec- and I do not hear anyone saying no.
If I were to vote for the amendment and the subamendment I would be saying, in effect, that these people ought to be supported in their vote of non-confidence against the government. Well, they cannot depend upon my vote, if they insist upon going ahead with the sort of suggestions they have been making in the past.
For instance, it was only recently that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) went ahead with his bill in which he insists upon imposing a divorce court upon the province of Quebec. Yet he knows perfectly well that Quebec has constitutional rights that they are ready to defend anywhere and at any time. So I repeat that the hon. member and his colleagues are not going to engage the confidence of the province of Quebec by acting in that way, and by trying to set aside those constitutional rights to which Quebec is entitled.
Then, other members of the C.C.F. have been making claims for federal grants for education in the provinces. This is another ground upon which federal members should not place their feet, because it touches one hundred per cent upon the autonomy of the provinces. Members of this house know very well that we are very ticklish about the question of autonomy.
After all, we have received some lessons that have taught us to be cautious, and not to do anything that would look like taking away or menacing the autonomy of any province. So I say to these gentlemen that if they wish to have the confidence of Quebec they will have to change their policy; they will have to mind their own business, in a way, and not try to take away from the province of Quebec those constitutional rights to which she is entitled.
We are often told that the federal government is trying to centralize. Well, I do not see suggestions for centralization coming as frequently from any quarter as it comes from hon. members on the opposite side of the house. I believe therefore that it would not be wise for me to give them my confidence, because I am not a centralizer. And because I am not a centralizer I am not going to vote with the champions of centralization in this country. Nor will I support those people who apparently do not know the first thing about all the measures they bring here affecting constitutional rights of citizens in this country.
The Budget-Mr. Dupuis
I have a few suggestions to make. When I rose in my place this evening I had no intention of trying to settle all the problems with which the government is faced. However, I did have a few observations to make and, as it is said in English, I shall proceed to get it off my chest. I hope in doing so I shall not hurt too deeply the feelings of hon. members in other parties. I speak only to explain my conduct, and to give my reasons for voting against the amendment and the subamendment, while at the same time offering some suggestions.
I have received many letters, some of which have come from unskilled workers asking for higher wages. These workers are earning at the present time 82 cents an hour. When one considers the high cost of living, he could not consider that a sufficient wage. The government ought to set an example by paying higher wages to those on low salaries, so that they may make both ends meet.
I know conditions are no worse than they have been under former governments, but it is my duty to ask for an increase, because I represent that class of workers, and I would not be doing my duty if, in my representations, I did not single them out.
As I have said before, there ought to be an upward revision of the salaries of civil servants in the lower grades. It may be that those in higher ranks earn enough so that they do not have serious financial problems. But this is not true of those in the lower grades, and it may be that some adjustment would be proper. I know, for instance, of some people doing a job in one department who find that they are paid less than those doing similar work in another department. Why should1 this condition remain?
These suggestions' are made in all good faith, and in the hope that at some time there may be a revision of the wages of the workers in these lower grades. I would hope that at some time we may have an end to all these war expenditures. There is no doubt, after all that it has done for the aged people, that this government will certainly take into consideration increasing the old age pension, other pensions and family allowances when war expenditures are not so heavy.
I would direct the attention of hon. members to the fact that $40 a month is not enough for the aged. I am sure every member on this side of the house will admit that they cannot go very far on $40. But, after all, it must be kept in mind that there have been some acts of amelioration by this government. There was a time when the aged were receiving only $20 a month. Then it was increased

The Budget-Mr. Dupuis to $30, and has finally reached $40. The age limit, which formerly stood at 65, is now placed at 70, and without a means test.
These things can be done step by step and I am quite sure in the near future the government will consider the advisability of amending the old age pensions, the family allowances, the veterans pensions and those paid to the C.N.R. employees and government employees. This government has shown its good will and its good intentions, and has actually carried out some of these changes.
I do compliment them for what they have done up to now, but I advise the ministers concerned not to stop where they are. They should give attention to the requests being made by these particular classes of people.
There is another matter about which I should like to speak. I do not want to exactly reproach the government about this, but I do want to say that I am not satisfied with the way cheques are sent out in the one language only. It would not cost much more to send out bilingual cheques. There are in my riding people named Smith, Warren and so on who cannot speak one word of English. They find it very diificult when they receive cheques or other documents in English.
I do not want to talk of my own personal affairs, but my wife was named Annie Rafferty and she cannot speak one word of English. Her grandfather who was bom in Ireland was brought up by a French family, in fact the family of Judge Cousineau in the city of Hull, and herself always lived in French-speaking circles and spoke French all the time and she just could not understand a document printed in English. I cannot see what good it does to send English documents to those with English names when it may be that they cannot speak English at all.
Just the other day I was speaking to a man in Ottawa named Lefebvre and he could not speak one word of French. I am not in favour of sending English documents to those with English names and French documents to those with French names when we could send out bilingual cheques which would be understood by everyone. In that way no mistakes would be made.
The next matter I want to take up is local in character, but it does have a bearing on the general situation throughout Canada. I refer to the tolls which are charged on the Jacques Cartier and Victoria bridges at Montreal. I understand that these are the only two bridges in Canada on which tolls are charged. The Victoria bridge has been paid for long ago. It is still quite narrow, although it was widened a few years ago. It is used considerably.


The Jacques Cartier bridge was built in 1930 and it showed deficits up to 1948 or 1949. But,, these deficits were not paid for by the dominion government alone; they were split among the federal government, the provincial government and the city of Montreal. As a result the city of Montreal has paid $2,850,000 up to date on the accumulated deficits on this bridge. As I say-, the tolls on all other bridges in Quebec and throughout Canada have been abolished. This is an anomaly which should be eliminated.
It is not fair to ask the people of Montreal and the suburbs to pay tolls when people using bridges in other parts of the country do not pay tolls. I will present a motion asking for the abolition of these tolls. If for some reason they cannot be abolished,
I would suggest that at least no charge be made for the passengers in the car. I know the Jacques Cartier bridge cost $21 million and there are still a few millions to be paid. If that charge was eliminated it would cost all the country only $233,000, which is not large as compared with $65 million for grain. That would give at least part justice to the residents of Montreal and the surrounding country.
If that cannot be done then I repeat the suggestion I made a few months ago that the province should be allowed to handle this bridge. Perhaps this could not be done in the case of the Victoria bridge because that is used by the Canadian National Railways, but the other bridge is only a highway bridge and it should be under the supervision of the roads department of the province of Quebec. If they were permitted to maintain the bridge it would settle all arguments. Part of the debt would have to be absorbed by Canada, but when you are thinking of justice you should not think only of figures. The chamber of commerce and other organizations in Montreal will be presenting petitions to the government to ask that this situation be corrected.
I do not know whether I should say this, but I am not invited to the caucuses of the Liberal party. That indicates that I am not considered to be a full member of the Liberal party. But I am old enough to have studied the history of my country and while there are many who may belong to political parties without knowing why-I am not referring only to Liberals-I know why I endorse this government. I have found that every time there has been prosperity in this country it was under a Liberal regime. It was under a Liberal administration. I do not know whether it is due to fate or bad administration on the part of the Conservative party but every time we have had a depression it has been when that party was in power. Therefore

why should I choose a party that always brings a depression with it when it is in power and cast aside a party that brings prosperity to the country?
I would not want to terminate my remarks without complimenting the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) on the honour recently bestowed upon them in having their names placed on a list of twenty-seven persons from among whom will be chosen the Nobel peace prize winner for 1951. The participation of the Prime Minister in the creation of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization and the part taken by these two Canadian statesmen certainly has been the reason for this distinction. I am sure I echo the views of every member of the house when I extend to them our sincere congratulations on this honour.

But I do not believe for a moment that it is necessary to touch our social services in order to alleviate the present burden of taxes on the majority of Canadians. Indeed, it is a matter of knowing how to apportion in a fair way the expense of government, now that we have an expenditure of over $2 billion for defence. If, for example, the government had imposed heavier increases in personal income taxes at the higher levels, and had imposed an excess profits tax on corporations, the burdens now oppressing the lower income groups certainly could have been reduced. I am sure if the hon. member for Moose Jaw had paused long enough to consider these points he would have adopted an entirely different approach to the subject of reductions in government expenditure.
I wish to go on record, as disagreeing with my colleague's contention that a means test should be applied under the Old Age Security Act and in regard to family allowances. In fairness to my colleague I should point out that he did not advocate a return to the old type of means test, but did suggest a ceiling of $5,000. Again I believe if the hon. member had stopped to think he would have seen only too clearly what would be the consequences of such a policy. We have opposed a means test under these and other social security measures in order to get away from the social stigma that is always attached to a person in "receipt of a pension given on a charitable basis. The removal of the means test did away with that stigma, and I am rather proud of the fact that it has been removed. I was very happy to learn that the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) had applied for his old age security pension, by that action indicating to everyone that he was not putting himself above his fellow Canadians. I think the Prime Minister is to be commended on this, and I only hope that everyone, whatever their status in life, will foHow his example.
As the house knows, we of the C.C.F. have always favoured an old age pension without a means test. Indeed we were the first to come out and advocate such a plan for our senior citizens. If we have any criticism of the old age pensions now in effect it is that they are inadequate. The present $40 is unrealistic, as it bears little or no relation to the high cost of living. For this reason we have urged that an old, age pension of $60 a month should be given everyone 65 years and over. The government wEl say we are not able to increase those pensions at this time. Others may point out that those in the lower and middle income brackets are already harassed by taxes they cannot now

afford to bear. With this last statement I am in entire agreement. The lower and middle income groups are not only bearing the burden of heavy personal income taxes; it is also they who are most adversely affected by the sales and excise taxes. While we commend the minister for altering the excise tax we cannot help but regret that he did not see fit to reduce the sales tax, for it is this indirect tax above all which oppresses so many Canadians who earn relatively small incomes.
The financing of old age security, for example, should not be made to bear heavily upon those in the lower levels of income, whom the pension was intended to help in the first place. There is no reason why those individuals who make above $3,000 taxable income should have that portion of their income exempt from the social security tax. Why should a person making $10,000 per year, or $20,000 or $50,000, as the case may be, pay a maximum of only $30 for the current year, the same as an individual with a taxable income of only $3,000? Certainly this is an unfair way to allocate the burden of this social security tax. It is on these points that we differ with the government. It is not a question of whether we are able to afford these things; rather it is a matter of apportioning them fairly so they do not hurt those least able to bear further tax increases. I believe in the principle of ability to pay.
With regard to family allowances I am happy to note that my colleague the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) has a resolution on the order paper calling for an increase in these allowances so they will have the same value they had when the act was introduced some years ago. This is another example of our endeavour to increase all social security payments so they will be brought into line with the present high cost of living.
The hon. member for Moose Jaw suggested reductions in civil service pensions. This does not coincide with the policy of our party or with my own views. On the contrary we have urged from time to time that these pensions be increased in view of the high cost of living. As it is now these pension rates, like other social security rates, are meaningless in this inflationary period. Certainly a majority of the members of this party support the efforts of the civil servants to get adequate pensions.
While I have expressed disagreement with some of the statements made by the hon. member for Moose Jaw, I must say he outlined several methods by which the government could save money, and with those
The Budget-Mr. Jones suggestions I heartily agree. I have in mind particularly his reference to the costly luxury of maintaining a lieutenant governor in each province, and his request for a survey of all personnel both military and civilian, with a view to eliminating waste and overlapping. No one objects to paying for security, but we strongly object to waste whether in material or in personnel. Savings can and must be made if we are to build up our defences and at the same time maintain our social security and other essential services.
In conclusion may I point out that sheer necessity has forced us into a position that calls for a budget of $4,500 million, the highest peacetime budget in our history. Last year it was slightly less, but the people paid up willingly and handsomely, and we wound up with a surplus of close to $700 million. They will do the same thing again. There may be some grumbling, but very little; and this has been the case because we recognize the emergency. Should we ever again be faced with domestic problems such as we faced in the thirties, never let it be said that we cannot find the money to ease the situation. That fallacy has gone forever, as we have proved in the last two years. We have done it now and we can do it again.
Finally I commend the government on its pay-as-you-go policy. I think that is a sound way to carry on. When the emergency is over the government will find that the people have higher incomes, and possibly they will have a billion or two not needed for defence which can then be used to build homes for the lower income groups, so capitalized that they can be owned outright in a period of ten or twenty years. Keep up the high rates of taxation for a year or two until the housing needs of all the people of Canada have been financed with the money now going into defence production at the rate of $2 billion a year.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
First, Mr. Speaker, I wish to congratulate the member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatcher) on the honest and able address he presented to this house last evening. I say that very sincerely because, as you know, my remarks are not always in praise of the government. For that reason, I realize it is not always easy to express one's honest opinion. Last evening we heard the member for Moose Jaw deliver a speech which rang with sincerity, and I believe he is to be congratulated by all those who were privileged to hear him.
For a few moments this evening I wish to deal with a problem that is perhaps outside my province, but one which has been misrepresented in this House of Commons. I

The Budget-Mr. A. W. Stuart refer to the cheese producers of Ontario. From information I have been able to obtain, I am convinced that it would be most difficult to arrive at a conclusion as to what this federal government could do about this situation which has been brought to the attention of the house on several occasions. The greater part of the cheese which is produced in Canada comes from an area between London, Ontario, and Three Rivers, Quebec, and the greater part of that would be manufactured in Ontario. May I remind the house that cheese is also produced in the maritime provinces, and the quality of that cheese is second to none. For that reason, I am making my few remarks at this time.
When I came to Ottawa in 1945 cheese was being marketed by the federal Department of Agriculture under a floor price which had been established under a wartime regulation in order that Britain's requirements would be met. From 1945 until 1950 this federal control was bitterly criticized by members sitting in the Progressive Conservative group. Their arguments were, and they are still on the record, that if cheese were taken from under federal control the price would automatically increase by 10, 20, 30 or 40-there were suggestions that it would even increase in value by 50 per cent. Month after month and year after year we listened to that criticism. In other words, the cheese producers did not appreciate this assistance from the federal Department of Agriculture. Consequently, two years ago, the Ontario cheese producers took the matter entirely out of the hands of the federal government. At this point I wish to add that the Ontario government had every right under our constitution to take this action. I believe no one would question their authority. I might add also that this is not the first time action of that type has been taken by the government of Ontario.
I remember some few years ago-I believe the leader of the official opposition (Mr. Drew) at the present time was the premier of Ontario then-it was decided the federal authorities had no judgment whatever so far as marketing Canadian products in Britain was concerned. There was a lot of comment in the press at that time, and it was very interesting reading. For that reason Ontario House was set up in the city of London. The staff was recommended and placed there by the government of Ontario. According to press reports at that time it appeared as though that organization would be able to sell ice to Eskimos. I could give another illustration. Shortly after the last war when we were bringing immigrants to this country from Europe, Ontario decided that the federal plan was outdated. The only thing that province could do was to set up its own system, 
and that was done. I do not believe we have any reason to criticize that action. I think the province had complete authority to do it. It would appear that on many occasions the government of Ontario has decided it was much more capable of handling problems than the federal government was. Again I say that I do not believe the federal government had any authority whatever to interfere in any of those activities I have mentioned.
Since the question of cheese production and marketing in Ontario has been discussed in this chamber on several occasions, I have endeavoured to find the answer to this problem. I am always interested in the welfare of the primary producers of this country. From information I have been able to obtain, it would appear that after the government of Ontario took the matter entirely out of the hands of the federal government-and this at the request of the cheese producers of Ontario-they established a floor price of 36 cents a pound for cheese. This action was taken just previous to the last provincial election. The results of that election would certainly indicate that the cheese producers of Ontario approved of the action taken by the provincial government. It would appear that the producers were happy over the 36 cents per pound floor price.
After the election, however, it was apparently found that the 36 cents per pound floor price was impossible to maintain. After having supplied the best markets in Canada these same producers, who were so dissatisfied with the treatment the federal department accorded them, again came to the federal government requesting it to take over their surplus production. This government is regularly criticized, and is now being criticized, for sunshine budgets just previous to elections and for lemon budgets just after elections. We have heard those expressions used in this chamber. After the ballots are counted, however, and. the results of a federal election are known, I would suggest that not a single case can be found where the federal government has ever gone to a provincial legislature requesting it to pull federal chestnuts out of the fire

in other words, passing the buck to the provincial legislature. It seems, however, that that does not apply when the shoe is on the other foot.
It would be most difficult and most unfair for the federal government to take over the surplus cheese in Ontario after, as I have said, the best markets have been supplied by this Ontario co-operative, and then have the federal department attempt to sell that surplus in competition with other cheese-producing provinces. The Ontario cheese producers asked the Ontario government for special

legislation to set up that co-operative to deal with cheese. The co-operative had the authority to compel delivery, and also to establish prices. If previous to the provincial election the floor price was set too high, why do the federal Progressive Conservative members now endeavour to hold the federal Department of Agriculture responsible? In my opinion this is an unfair advantage to try to take in this House of Commons. Under our constitution-and, I might say also, at the request of the cheese producers of Ontario -this is purely a problem for the legislature of that province. It in no way relates to this government.
Last year the Minister of Finance increased the tax on cigarettes. At the same time he placed a special tax on stoves, refrigerators and other household appliances. After a fair trial, which was a year, he decided-in this budget which was just brought down a few days ago-to remove the amount of the increase of 1951. Why does the provincial government of the province of Ontario refuse to acknowledge their mistake with regard to cheese? The federal Conservative members endeavoured to place the full responsibility for this mistake at the door of the Department of Agriculture here in Ottawa.
In conclusion, might I say that the Ontario government has established a floor price. This same organization compels the producers of cheese to deliver their product to the provincial co-operatives. Why should the federal government try to establish another floor price which would undoubtedly be below the one set by the provincial government of Ontario? Then the federal Progressive Conservative members could stand up and say: Your federal Department of Agriculture is responsible for the reduction in the price of cheese. To my mind, that is exactly the thing they are working for at the present time. I feel that the Department of Agriculture has every right in the world to deny them that privilege. To begin with, the federal government have no legal authority to do this, and I would not approve the federal government's going into the cheese business, not only in competition with the Ontario board but also with all other Canadian producers.
This information that I have taken a few minutes to put on the record this evening is a true picture of the action taken by the cheese producers of Ontario since 1945. Those who have criticized the federal Department of Agriculture for present-day conditions in the industry are well aware of the fact that they are dealing with a matter which is purely a problem for the provincial government of the province of Ontario and not for the federal Department of Agriculture.
The Budget-Mr. Nowlan

speechtext: Will you reduce your speeches to thirty minutes?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I will on this occasion, at any rate. However, Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak on this matter of the budget, I first should like to congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) on the, as some others have said, admirable footwork which he displayed in delivering his address. Certainly it was a physical task of considerable dimension, as we all realize. I think he spoke for almost two hours in a way which held the interest of the house and reflected credit on himself at least in so far as the manner of his delivery was concerned. While I am speaking on manner of delivery, may I say that I think perhaps an encomium of praise should be passed out to the parliamentary assistant who spoke later on in the debate and who formerly on some occasions, like Don Quixote tilting at windmills, aimed his lance at every person who stuck his head up beyond the desk in this house and struck at him at least loudly and violently, if not always wisely. On this occasion he showed discretion, discrimination and a statesmanlike approach which suggested to me that he felt that possibly the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Sinnott) had developed such talents as a financial critic that his position as financial assistant was in jeopardy and that in the case of the retirement of the present minister, possibly the hon. member for Springfield would be made minister of finance, rather than the parliamentary assistant. I think that consideration is undoubtedly responsible for that temperate display which we witnessed here the day before yesterday.
I am, of course, not going to refer to all of the happy allusions and appellations which have been used, from "Abbott's rabbit" to a score of others, or to what some have called a Hallowe'en budget. But certainly when the minister referred to this illusory reduction
1S28

The Budget-Mr. Nowlan of income tax, I remembered that ditty which some of us heard many years ago:
Last night I met upon the stair A little man who wasn't there.
He wasn't there again today.
My, how I wish he'd go away!
I am sure the reduction of 6 per cent which was presaged in the early part of the speech was something like this illusory man of which we have heard.
There is certainly no question that this country is suffering from a tremendous load of taxation. I am not going into the merits of that matter tonight, except to reiterate what was pointed out by the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) the other day, namely, that the reductions which were made and for which the minister took credit, were reductions of taxes which had been protested a year ago by the financial critic of the opposition, the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell), the ho.n. member for Eglinton and all others on this side of the house. It is true that certain reductions have been made, but those were reductions in taxes which never should have been imposed in the first place.
When one today sees someone attempting to take credit for having reduced these taxes, shall we say, on electrical appliances, one must also think of those unfortunate young people who perhaps during this year have married, established homes for themselves, have bought those appliances with those additional taxes imposed on them, and who now find that through a vagary or a Whim of the Minister of Finance, someone else who has established a home this year fortunately will be able to replace them or buy them without paying the same taxes. Certainly there has been placed on some of those people a burden which I do not think they will forget too soon.
Not only is this tax burden a heavy one which, as the hon. member for Greenwood pointed out the other day, amounts to $1,715 or more than that on the head of every family in Canada, in federal taxes alone. That is a substantial burden. People talk about this country being prosperous today. They talk about the bank deposits. I am sure that some of these bank deposits' will increase on the 30th of this month when some of us have to go to the bank and borrow money with which to pay our income taxes. In the return for that month you will perhaps find a substantial increase in the bank deposits, but I think that most of us will find that it is an exceedingly illusory one indeed.
I want to speak for a moment about the way in which this tax is applied, with

regard to the primary producers, the farmers
and the fishermen who, as all those conversant with the act realize, have the so-called right to average their taxation over a period of years. I am not going into the technical provisions of that act, Mr. Speaker; but as most hon. members perhaps know, there were two prerequisites. First, you have to file your return on time every year; and that is certainly a proper one. Second, you must afterwards make application. You must apply for the right to average. I am suggesting this. If the farmer or fisherman is entitled to average if he files his return properly, why should he be debarred from taking advantage of that right merely because of his technical default in making application before the 30th day of April in any particular year? What it means is this. The primary producer-the farmer or the fisherman- who has a large income or who possibly has had in other years, and has to hire an accountant or someone with business experience to make out his return for him, is advised of that provision. He makes his application, and thereby can save a substantial amount of money over the years in payment of his income tax. But someone else who does not know of that provision, a smaller farmer or fisherman, who is not in the financial position to employ auditors, perhaps does not know about that. In this way he is debarred. And even those who do know about it sometimes suffer inadvertently.
I can think of one primary producer who employed an auditor to make out his income tax return. This auditor had done so for years. He had an application for averaging. But apparently, on the night of April 30, he forgot to mail it, and did not mail it until the first of May. As a result of that, this farmer suffered an increased tax of over $1,800. That was the result because of this default on the part of a person, one who possibly is responsible in damages in a civil action, if it were instituted. Nevertheless it was not the fault of the producer.
I am suggesting that the act should be amended so that those primary producers should have, as of right, the opportunity to average without having to go through the technical process of making application therefor.
And in that connection I wish to make one reference to the practice in connection with these income tax returns of primary producers on a net worth statement. The farmer will file an income tax return honestly and properly, but the department may raise some objection, or may feel that the returns

have not been properly prepared. They investigate that man's affairs, they prepare a statement of net worth, and the farmer is assessed on the amount they state. He faces a situation-and this could apply to a fisherman- where he must either pay on the statement of net worth, or lodge an appeal. Usually the amounts involved are such, and the distances from courts are such, that the persons affected just cannot appeal.
I must say that although I believe most of the officials in the department are fair and reasonable, I doubt if they all are. And in some cases I think they have been most unreasonable. Let us consider for a moment the situation of a farmer in my own constituency, where their apple trees were removed and where, because of the loss of the British market, the returns from the orchards have tremendously depreciated. Yet, in a net worth statement those orchards are carried at exactly the same value as they were in 1944 or 1945, the original year when they started the net worth provision.
They refuse to reduce those values. And if a farmer has received money in respect of trees pulled out, those capital sums are included in income, so that the poor farmer loses in both ways. His farm is maintained at the same artificial value, although he has no trees, because the trees were removed. And then the money he got for the trees is included in income. There is a situation such as that in connection with this net worth statement. I suggest the department should make careful investigation, and that certainly some change should be made.
Now, departing from that phase of the matter, and returning to the budget, as such: The parliamentary assistant the other day, closing his remarks, referred with not unbecoming modesty to the wonderful position in which this country finds itself, and he asked if there was anyone anywhere who could boast of living under happier circumstances than the people of this country.
Well, I wonder if that applies to the farmers of Canada today. I wonder if those who, shall I say, are growing beef in this country, with their market in the United States lost to them, are facing the situation with that high degree of equanimity and satisfaction to which the parliamentary assistant refers. I wonder if those who are in the poultry business are in that happy frame of mind.
Only the other day I talked to a farmer who, to a rather considerable extent, has been engaged in poultry raising. In other words, he was operating a one-man poultry farm. He told me he formerly employed help to the extent of two or three people, and
The Budget-Mr. Nowlan informed me further that, by discharging his help and doing all the work himself, at the present price of eggs he could pay himself about $2 a day wages. But he told me that if the price of eggs dropped another cent he would not be able to pay himself even that much. I do not think he would join in this paean of praise in which the parliamentary assistant indulged the other day.
And would those who are engaged in the dairy industry? Do they feel about it that way? Certainly the apple producers in the east and in the west who are facing loss of market, and a chaotic situation generally, are not too happy about it. They are not too pleased with the situation in Canada today.
I am sure there are many others employed in various lines of industry who would not share his views. For instance, let us consider the textile industry. I do not think they would say Amen to all that was said the other day by the parliamentary assistant. The same would be true in eastern Canada in respect of almost every category of employment.
It is all right to talk about figures. There is no doubt that the figures supplied by the dominion bureau of statistics show increases in bank deposits, in savings and in wages. That is all very fine. The figures are there, and no one questions that on an average they represent a satisfactory situation in many places. But neither could there be any question that, in respect of the citizen in the white-collar class, or the man on a pension, or the teacher, or the clerk-indeed, the great army of people who have no unions representing them, and who perhaps have no spokesmen speaking on their behalf-it would be true to say that they are being crushed today by the burden of taxation, a burden which for them has become almost unbearable.
They do not find the situation as happy as one might think. And speaking of the dairy farmer, may I refer again to a matter which may be only of local interest, although I think it has wider implications. All hon. members know what happened last year in the United States when the American congress added a rider to an appropriation bill placing an embargo on the importation of cheese.
We do know that our government has moved very softly in the matter-and I think properly so-in the hope that an adjustment will be made. And possibly it will be made. Certainly in so far as the executive branch of government in that country is concerned, there can be no question but that there is a wish to rectify the situation. But sooner or later, Mr. Speaker, our government may

The Budget-Mr. Nowlan made available, and quite properly so. Assistance can be obtained tor the western wheat grower. Their plight only has to be raised on the floor of the house and our friends from the western provinces close ranks. Then inside of a week or two weeks the necessary moneys are voted and it is all over.
We hear these terrible sobs and cries from western members about the plight of the western farmer. We appreciate their plight and sympathize with it, but I think those of us from the east on all sides of the house sometimes feel that our own primary producers have suffered disasters and have not received the treatment which wouldi have been accorded them if they had happened to live in another part of Canada. Last year the fishermen off the Atlantic coast did not suffer a disaster because of a storm but they just did not catch any fish. There were none, and they did not come appealing to the house for help. Now, however, there is a situation which requires attention.
When the minister was in Nova Scotia the other day he made a suggestion which I think is a constructive one and may have some merit. He suggested the working out of some form of insurance with respect to these things. But let us get some action on these matters, and I suggest that we want to avoid internecine feuds and wrangles and get a clear-cut policy between the federal and provincial governments so that in the matter of storm relief as well as other matters there may be more direct action in the future. These jurisdictional wrangles are of interest with respect to another matter which I have mentioned before. I will not say I feel deeply about it because it is a matter of viewpoint or perhaps a matter of the imagination. However, I want to refer to it because the solution of the problems of those of us from the east-and we have our problems- is centred to a certain extent upon the development of power.
With the Canso bridge going in and the satisfactory development of the steel industry, I believe we can have primary industries and that secondary industries will follow. This will go a long way toward solving the economic problems of the maritimes. However, we need power, and I have enough vision, perhaps enough Irish in me and enough speculative imagination to think that the development of atomic energy may be the solution of our power problems in the maritimes. Obviously that form of power will not be desired by the central provinces within the next few years because they are going to invest so much money in the development of hydroelectric energy. Therefore they will have to safeguard their investment and will not want to see the development of

power from atomic energy take place too rapidly in central Canada. Therefore we will have the opportunity of developing the use of atomic power in the east along the Atlantic coast. I was speaking the other day to a gentleman who is very close to this matter. He is one whose name you all know and he did not only say this to me but to many others. He said publicly that the development of atomic energy in Canada was such that one could visualize it in the same way as if the Kitty Hawk plane of Orville Wright's days were transformed within three years into a big United States bomber of the last war. He said if you could envisage such a transformation you could get a picture of the development of atomic energy in the industrial field that they can foresee today. All that has been done within these past few years. If we have no internecine feuds between the provinces and the federal government, if we can get the use of atomic power developed in the maritimes, then I suggest these provinces will again take the position in the economy of the country which they had before confederation when they really carried the country. Possibly our friends from the central Canadian provinces, who today are enjoying such tremendous wealth, may find that they will be only cousins although perhaps not poor cousins. They will find that our standard of prosperity will be equivalent to that maintained in the rest of Canada.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate I do so with considerable knowledge of how many residents of my constituency feel about the budget presented by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott). I can assure you that I am not going to try to describe it in the house. In the first place I would not want to, and in the second place, Mr. Speaker, I am sure you would not allow me to do so.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Give it a trial.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
However, they were very disappointed. They say it is a very disappointing budget. The people who pay personal income taxes were sadly disappointed. After listening to the minister say that we were going to get a 6 per cent reduction in income tax it certainly upset them to find there was an increase. I believe the figures that have appeared in most of our daily papers are correct. There is no need for me to go over them again. The minister and his parliamentary assistant know them quite well.
I listened to a speech tonight with which I must take issue, that of the hon. member for St. Mary (Mr. Dupuis). He spoke about western farmers getting so much from the provinces of Quebec and Ontario. He did not

mention the $65 million but he hinted at it and we knew very well what he meant. May I suggest to the hon. member that he look at the record and find out the losses that the grain growers of the west, wheat growers in particular, have suffered during the last few years. He may have often wondered why you can buy bread so cheaply. I would not be a bit surprised at that. The reason for that is that the farmers, who comprise one-third of the population of this country, subsidized the rest of the country by supplying cheap wheat. I think that is a statement that cannot very well be contradicted. The wheat farmers of the west are in a very precarious position today. As a matter of fact they do not know just what to do. The year 1951 was a good growing but a bad harvesting year. In the province of Alberta today approximately 56 million bushels of wheat and 71 million bushels of coarse grains still remain unthreshed. When a province suffers in that way it is a national disaster. It is true that in parts of Alberta they are doing some threshing and some of the wheat is turning out not too badly, but it must be remembered also that in the southern part of the province, from a line drawn south from Red Deer, we have had more rain than for many years. All the lakes are full; the sloughs are full, and the fields are under water. Much of that crop is ruined.
I am not blaming the federal government for that, of course, but I am suggesting there is something wrong when a member from one of the eastern provinces gets up in this house and says we are giving the western farmers so much money. I would ask the house, if it had not been for western Canada where would the Cocksfautt Plow Company be, where would the Massey-Harris Company be, where would the International Harvester Company be, and many others? In my travels around Ottawa I still have to see as much machinery as is used out west. In the smaller villages in this vicinity I have not seen machinery piled in the yards as it is out in Saskatchewan and Alberta. It must be remembered that all this machinery is produced in Ontario and Quebec, yet the best market for it is in the western provinces. What about cars? When we buy a car at home we pay $226 freight from Oshawa to Medicine Hat on a Chevrolet, the cheapest car you can buy. Ontario people can go to Oshawa and pick up a car without paying any freight. The trouble is that we are hooked both ways. We pay the freight on our grain to the head of the lakes and we pay the freight on our cars and machinery from the point of distribution to the point of delivery.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
And all the freight goes to Ontario and Quebec.
The Budget-Mr. Wylie

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is something the eastern members must realize. It is something many of them do not appreciate. When the dominion government, or should I say the wheat board, was prepared to pay the western farmers $65 million of their own money, why should the west be criticized for accepting it? Don't try to tell me that money came out of taxes. If that was the case I would like the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance to tell me so. I believe that came out of the wheat board.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It came directly out of the farmers.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Certainly it came out of the farmers; it was their own money. Every time we hear that sort of thing in the house I really boil over, because it is not fair; it is not playing the game, and it is not helping bring about the unity we should have in this country. We know very well we cannot get along without the east. Surely the east must know they cannot get along without us.
Then just a word about coarse grains. What about the freight on coarse grains that has been paid by the government? We do not hear very much about that, though I remember that one night the right hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) spoke to the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Fulford) about it and put him in his place. When the minister speaks he usually knows what he is talking about. He certainly did that night, because he showed exactly what the farmers in Ontario and Quebec had received by way of freight assistance on feed grains.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: $110 million.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It was twice that. We do not object to that. If the government wants to do it that is its affair, but that money comes out of the taxes we pay. When the farmers out west received $65 million from the wheat board that was their own money, and they were entitled to a lot more than that. They should have received many more times that amount.
Today the wheat farmers are paying too much for what they buy and getting too little for what they sell. We hear about the cost of living coming down. Sure it has come down, but on what? On what the farmer produces. It is true that if you buy a new car today the price has dropped somewhat. All the government did was to take off 10 per cent in excise tax. But today many people cannot afford to buy new cars. Many farmers cannot afford them this year; they
1634	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Wylie did not get their grain threshed last year and may not get it threshed this year. I would suggest to the government that it is about time the wheat board gave the farmers a little more for their wheat; and it is just about time one-third of the population, making up our basic industry of agriculture, stopped subsidizing the rest of the people so they can have cheap bread.
We have heard a lot about family allowances, old age security and almost everything else in this debate. Sometimes it does not hurt to repeat what has been said; but in view of the fact that it is going to take me considerable time and I cannot possibly finish by eleven o'clock, I move the adjournment of the debate.
Motion agreed to and debate adjourned.
